faqs.q: Do I need approval to build on my rural block?
faqs.a:
Almost certainly yes. A new house, shed, or carport needs building approval, and depending on the site it may also need planning approval (the two are different — see the next question).

A very short list of minor structures don't require building approval under Schedule 2 of the Queensland Building Regulation 2021 — generally garden sheds under 10m², some retaining walls under 1m, and fences under 2m. These are called accepted development (self-assessable), meaning no permit is needed but you are still responsible for complying with the Building Code of Australia, boundary setbacks, and the Planning Scheme.

Don't rely on a summary for your specific project. What counts as exempt depends on exact dimensions, location on the lot, overlays, and what's already on the property. If in doubt, call 1300 697 372 before spending money — getting this wrong can mean rebuilding.

Reference: Building Regulation 2021 — Schedule 2.

faqs.q: What's the difference between building approval and planning approval?
faqs.a:
These sound similar but answer two different questions:

  • Planning approval asks: can this use happen on this land? It's about where the building goes, how it's sited, and whether the use fits the Planning Scheme. Rules include setbacks, road access, watercourse distances, overlays (flood, bushfire), and proximity to things like quarries or feedlots.
  • Building approval asks: is the structure itself safe and compliant? It's about how the building is constructed — footings, framing, bracing, tie-down, energy efficiency, smoke alarms, and all the engineering that makes the building safe.

Many rural blocks only need building approval, because the Planning Scheme already sets out acceptable outcomes — if your chosen house site ticks every box on the Building a House in the Rural Zone checklist, no planning approval is required and you can go straight to building approval.

If your site doesn't tick every box (e.g. in the bushfire zone, or unable to meet setbacks), you'll need planning approval first — specifically a Material Change of Use (MCU) application — and then building approval.

faqs.q: How do I check whether my rural site is suitable before I spend money?
faqs.a:
Two free tools — used together — will tell you most of what you need to know before you talk to anyone.

  1. SDRC Online Mapping. Open the Online Mapping tool, search your address, and switch on the Planning module. This confirms your zone (Rural, Rural Residential, etc.) and lets you toggle overlays — flood hazard, bushfire hazard, water resource catchment, airport environs etc. When your chosen house site is within certain overlays, extra requirements are triggered.
  2. Rural Zone Checklist. Work through the Building a House in the Rural Zone checklist. It covers the "acceptable outcomes" (AOs) — setbacks, slope, flood-free building site, water storage, separation from quarries / feedlots / abattoirs, energy supply, and overlay-specific requirements.

If you can tick every item on the checklist, you don't need planning approval — just building approval. If any item can't be ticked, the site may still be buildable, but it will need planning approval (Material Change of Use Application) first. See the question below for more information. 


Rural Zone setbacks

Zone Class 1a (dwellings) Class 10a (sheds, garages, carports)
Rural Zone 60m from all boundaries if gravel road frontage OR 6m from front & 60m from side & rear (if bitumen frontage) (or planning approval required) 6m from front boundary, regardless of road surface. 1.5m side & rear boundaries (or siting concession required)

Rural setbacks also interact with various factors such as watercourses, animal industries, slope, and the size of a flood-free building pad. The combination is specific to each block, so for anything beyond the basics please call Council's building team on 1300 697 372 and they'll walk you through what applies to your land.

faqs.q: What if my site doesn't meet the Rural Zone Checklist?
faqs.a:
You apply for a Material Change of Use (MCU) — a planning approval that assesses your proposal against the Planning Scheme's performance outcomes rather than the strict acceptable outcomes.

MCU (Material Change of Use): a type of planning application for when a land use is starting, restarting, or intensifying. Applies here because rural houses that can't meet all the acceptable outcomes become code assessable — they need planning approval before building approval.

If a performance outcome can be met another way, approval is typically granted with conditions. For example, if there's no constructed road, a condition will be to construct one. Another example, if there's a nearby quarry, conditions may require building orientation or materials that reduce dust/noise impact.

What a simple MCU needs:

  • Application form (DA Form 1) and fees
  • Written landowner consent
  • Supporting information — how you'll design, construct and operate, plus a statement addressing the Planning Scheme
  • Specific details for any checklist item you don't comply with

A simple MCU takes around 20 business days to decide. Longer if an information request is issued or a Referral Agency is involved (in relation to your application, Council may need information from the State Government), or the application requires impact assessment.

Detailed guidance: How to Make a Material Change of Use 

MCUs are technical. For anything beyond the simplest case, consider engaging a private town planning consultant — or book a Pre-Lodgement Meeting with Council's Town Planners ($300, up to 1 hour) for tailored advice regarding your specific application. General enquiries are free, call 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner.

faqs.q: Where do I start?
faqs.a:
For building in the Rural Zone, here's a short protocol for your first week:

  1. First choose a house site and determine the type of structure that you intend to build. Rural blocks tend to have many potential house sites, some more suitable than others. Likewise, different structure types (new build, prefabricated, removal home, etc) have their pros and cons to consider. Having a rough idea what type of structure you intend to build and where you intend to build it greatly assists with determining approval requirements and assists with getting quotes from contractors. 
  2. Next check whether planning approval is required. Open the Online Mapping tool and confirm your property is planning zoned as rural. Then use the mapping tool to work through the Rural Zone Checklist to determine if your property requires planning approval. Mark each item ✓ / ✗ / NA.
  3. If any item is ✗, call Council on 1300 697 372 and ask to arrange a callback from the planning department, customer service will take the details and arrange a call with a town planner (general enquiries have no financial cost and are commitment free). Have your address, and the building in the rural zone checklist with any ✗ items ready to discuss. You don't have to know all the terminology before you ring, that's what the duty planner is there for.
  4. Begin to get quotes from licensed builders to establish a rough idea of what is possible within your budget and to get an idea of the possible timeline. If going that route, this is a good time to engage a private certifier. See question below for more information. 
It is not uncommon for private professionals to have a preferred network, for example, a builder may prefer to work with a certain architect, building certifier, plumber etc. Which professionals you choose to work with is ultimately your decision.

faqs.q: Should I use a private certifier or Council for building approval?
faqs.a:
Building certifier: a QBCC-licensed professional who checks the building work against the Building Act, the National Construction Code, the Queensland Development Code, and the relevant Australian Standards. They decide the application, arrange inspections, and issue the Form 21 Final Certificate at the end. You can hire a private certifier or use Council as your certifier — the choice is yours.

Council as certifier: You prepare and lodge the application yourself (or with your builder's help). Council handles the assessment and inspections. Usually cheaper overall, but more work for you.

Private certifier: most larger projects go this route. The certifier prepares and lodges the application for you, and usually subcontracts extra professionals as needed (engineers, surveyors, soil tests, energy efficiency report, BAL report), liaises with Council on your behalf, and conducts on-site inspections. Council fees are the same either way — the certifier charges their own professional fee on top.

Many people find a private certifier is worth the fee — they can catch missing documents before lodgement and optimise the construction schedule to the certification process. As the applicant, it is your decision what will work best for you.

faqs.q: What are the setback requirements?
faqs.a:
Setbacks — how far a building has to sit from each boundary — depends on the zone of your land and the class of building. For rural land, the two classes most property owners need to know about are:

  • Class 1a Dwelling — a habitable structure designed for long-term habitation such as new house builds, prefabricated structures, removal homes etc.  
  • Class 10a Outbuilding — a non-habitable structure, not designed for people to live in such as a shed, garage, carport, or workshop, 

In the Rural Zone, dwellings and outbuildings have different setbacks:

Zone Class 1a (dwellings) Class 10a (sheds, garages, carports)
Rural Zone If gravel road frontage, 60m from all boundaries. If sealed road 6m from front & 60m from side & rear (or planning approval required) 6m from front boundary, regardless of road surface. 1.5m side & rear boundaries (or siting concession required)

Class 1a dwellings — the 60m setback from every boundary on a gravel road is the rule most people are surprised by. It reflects the Planning Scheme's intent to keep rural dwellings well clear of unconstructed roads and neighbouring rural operations. Bitumen frontage gives a shorter front setback (6m), but side and rear remain at 60m. If your block can't meet either pattern, planning approval is required (see the MCU question above).

Class 10a outbuildings — sheds, garages and carports follow the same residential-style rule regardless of road surface. If you can't meet 6m front or 1.5m side/rear, a siting concession can be applied for as part of the building application.

Other things that commonly affect where you can build on rural land include items such as watercourse separations, distances from animal industries, slope, and a flood-free building site. These don't change the setback rule above, but they do narrow down where on the block the approval rules can be satisfied. If in doubt, call 1300 697 372 and request a call back from Council's Town Planning team to help determine the optimal building position. 

Rural Residential zone setbacks aren't shown here — the rules differ slightly from Rural Zone. If your land is Rural Residential (this can be confirmed by searching the address on the Online Mapping tool) call Council's building team on 1300 697 372 for the correct values.

faqs.q: What documents do I need to lodge a building application for a new rural house?
faqs.a:
For a Class 1a dwelling (new house or extension), the full lodgement package is:

  • Completed DA Form 2 (the QLD Government building development application form)
  • Site Plan, Floor Plan, Elevations, and Structural Details
  • Footing / Slab Design with Form 15 signed by a Registered Professional Engineer of Queensland (RPEQ)
  • Soil Test Report
  • Energy Efficiency Report (houses must meet 7-Star)
  • Bushfire Attack Level (BAL) Report — if the site is in the Bushfire Hazard Overlay
  • QBCC Insurance Certificate if using a licensed builder and the work is $3,300 or more; or QBCC Owner Builder Permit if building yourself and the work is $11,000 or more
  • QLeave payment receipt if the build is valued at $150,000 or more (excl. GST)

Council's Building Info Sheets list the full requirements. Incomplete applications are rejected, so it's worth checking the appropriate fact sheet before lodging.

You cannot commence any building work until you have received the Decision Notice (Approval). Starting early — even clearing or pouring footings — creates unapproved work that has to be undone or retrospectively certified at your cost.

faqs.q: What documents do I need to lodge a building application for a new shed?
faqs.a:
For a Class 10a shed, the full lodgement package is:

  • Completed DA Form 2 (the QLD Government building development application form)
  • Site Plan, Floor Plan, Elevations, and Structural Details
  • Footing / Slab Design with Form 15 signed by a Registered Professional Engineer of Queensland (RPEQ)
  • Form 15 Certificate for the steel frame (signed by an RPEQ)
  • QBCC Insurance Certificate if using a licensed builder and the work is $3,300 or more; or QBCC Owner Builder Permit if building yourself and the work is $11,000 or more
  • QLeave payment receipt if the build is valued at $150,000 or more (excl. GST)

A soil test isn't required by default for a shed — one may be needed where the footing design calls for it, or where an engineering or on-site sewerage/plumbing approval applies.

Key differences from a Class 1a house application: a shed doesn't need an energy efficiency report. It still needs a BAL report if in the Bushfire Hazard Overlay and located within 6m of a residence.

When you later apply for the house, it's a separate Class 1a application with the full document list. The shed doesn't "count" toward the house approval — they're assessed independently.


Council's Building Info Sheets list the full requirements. Incomplete applications are rejected, so it's worth checking the appropriate fact sheet before lodging.

You cannot commence any building work until you have received the Decision Notice (Approval). Starting early — even clearing or pouring footings — creates unapproved work that has to be undone or retrospectively certified at your cost.

faqs.q: What about sewerage? Do I need a septic tank or a treatment plant?
faqs.a:
Most rural properties are not connected to Council's sewerage network, so you'll need an On-Site Sewerage Facility (OSSF) to treat wastewater on your own land. There are two main options:

  • Septic tank with an absorption trench — the traditional approach. Wastewater flows into the tank, solids settle, and liquid effluent disperses through trenches into the soil. Works well on well-draining land with adequate room for the trenches.
  • Aerated Wastewater Treatment System (AWTS) — treats wastewater to a higher standard using aeration, which allows treated water to be dispersed over a smaller area, often via surface irrigation. Costs more to install and requires ongoing servicing, but is often the only option on smaller or difficult sites.

Which is right for your block depends on soil type, lot size, slope, separation from watercourses, bores and neighbours, and the number of bedrooms. A soil test and a consultation with a licensed plumber are the two things that will give you a clear answer. Don't commit to a house design before this — the sewerage solution can influence building footprint and siting.

OSSF installations require Council plumbing approval before work begins, and inspections during construction. Full detail and application forms: On-Site Sewerage Facilities (OSSF) — SDRC.

faqs.q: What if I'm building a shed first, then a house later?
faqs.a:
This is a common pathway on the Southern Downs — build the shed first to store equipment and materials during the build, then build the permanent house later. Both stages still need proper approval, but the process is similar for both.

A shed (Class 10a — sheds, garages, carports) requires its own building application with a smaller checklist of documents than a new dwelling: 

  • Completed DA Form 2
  • Site Plan, Floor Plan, Elevations, and Structural Details
  • Footing / Slab Design with Form 15 signed by an RPEQ
  • Form 15 Certificate for the steel frame (signed by an RPEQ)
  • QBCC Insurance Certificate or Owner Builder Permit as above
  • QLeave receipt if the shed is valued at $150,000 or more (excl. GST)

A soil test isn't required by default for a shed — one may be needed where the footing design calls for it, or where an engineering or on-site sewerage/plumbing approval applies.

Key differences from a Class 1a house application: a shed doesn't need an energy efficiency report. It still needs a BAL report if in the Bushfire Hazard Overlay and located within 6m of a residence.

When you later apply for the house, it's a separate Class 1a application with the full document list. The shed doesn't "count" toward the house approval — they're assessed independently.

faqs.q: What about tiny homes, prefabricated houses, or shipping container builds?
faqs.a:
Short answer: a smaller or alternative building does not mean less approval. The most common misconception is that "tiny" or "prefab" means the normal rules don't apply. They do.

Tiny homes

Fixed to the land. Whether prefabricated or built on site, a tiny home permanently fixed to the land and used as a primary or secondary home is treated like any other Class 1a dwelling. Same building approval process, same document list, same inspections, same Form 21 at the end. Council removed the minimum 60m² floor area requirement in August 2024, so there's no "too small" threshold for a Class 1 dwelling in the Southern Downs.

On wheels. Treated like caravans. They can be stored on the land without approval if they're genuinely just being stored (not lived in, not connected to utility services). Living in one on your land is only permitted under a Temporary Home permit (see the question below about living on the land during construction).

Prefabricated and manufactured homes

Can be approved as Class 1a dwellings, but the paperwork is often harder — not easier. Many commercially sold tiny homes and modular units are imported and may not meet Australian standards. Before buying, ask the supplier for written certification that building, plumbing and electrical works meet Queensland requirements, including RPEQ signoff. Things a certifier will want to verify include structural adequacy, ceiling height, energy efficiency (7-Star rating), termite barriers, damp and weatherproofing, fire safety, Form 15 for structural elements, Form 43 for waterproofing, and the ability to get QBCC insurance. If these certifications can't be produced, a building approval may not be obtainable — and without one, a Form 21 can't be issued.

Shipping containers

Depends entirely on the intended use:

  • Self-assessable (no approval): temporary short-term storage (under 6 months) on residential land during renovations or removals, provided it's not fixed to the ground, not on a road or road reserve, and doesn't affect community amenity. Also self-assessable for short-term storage on industrial, rural, or active construction sites.
  • Building approval required: any use as an outbuilding (office, shed, workshop, hobby room etc); any use as a structure (fence, viewing platform, architectural feature); long-term storage (over 6 months); anchored to the ground with footings, slabs, electricity or plumbing; or altered with doors, windows, awnings, or attachments.
  • Amenity & Aesthetics application: required before building approval when the container is in any Urban or Rural Residential zone, or in the Rural zone if within 100m of a residential area, on a lot 4,000m² or less, or within 20m of a property boundary. Conditions commonly imposed include painting, concrete slab or 400mm stumps (to prevent rabbit harbourage — a Darling Downs Moreton Rabbit Board requirement), and sometimes a pitched roof.

Council has dedicated fact sheets on both tiny houses and shipping containers. Given how specific the rules are to each situation, please call Council on 1300 697 372 before committing funds — a 10-minute conversation can save thousands.

faqs.q: What about removal homes (relocated houses)?
faqs.a:
Removal homes are popular in the region and have their own approval pathway — as well as a building approval, Council acts as a Concurrence Agency, assesses the house's condition and appearance, and requires a security bond before the house can be moved.

The process is different enough that it has its own tab: see Removal Homes for the full journey — what to check before buying, the two applications, bond amounts and refunds, transport permits, and the inspections after the house arrives.

faqs.q: Do I need approval for my driveway?
faqs.a:
Yes — almost certainly. The issue is that any new or upgraded driveway has to cross Council land (the road reserve — the strip between your property boundary and the road itself) to reach the road, and Section 75(2) of the Local Government Act prohibits carrying out works on a road without Council's permission. That permission is called a Works Within Road Reserve approval. It's separate from, and in addition to, your building approval.

Road reserve: also called the nature strip, this is the full width of land set aside for a road, including the sealed or gravelled surface, any verge or shoulder, table drains, and the strip to the property boundary. It's all Council-managed land, even though the verge and table drain may look like part of your property.

When you need a Works Within Road Reserve approval:

  • New driveway access (part of virtually every new build)
  • Widening or relocating an existing driveway
  • Changing the driveway surface — for example, upgrading from gravel to bitumen or concrete
  • Any earthworks or culvert work in the road reserve (including filling in a table drain or installing a new culvert pipe)

What's involved:

  • Complete the Application Minor Works — Works Within a Road Reserve form from Council's Engineering Department
  • Attach a sketch plan showing the proposed location of the works within the road reserve
  • Pay the application fee — see the current Fees & Charges schedule
  • Allow 20 working days for assessment
  • On approval, Council issues an Approval Letter setting out the terms and conditions under which work can proceed

Rural-specific things to know:

  • Longer driveways often need a culvert where the driveway crosses the table drain, so water can continue to flow. Culvert size and placement are part of the approval assessment.
  • Gravel driveways need approval too — the rule is about works on the road reserve, not about whether the driveway is sealed.
  • If your property accesses the New England Highway, Cunningham Highway, or another state-controlled road, driveway access is assessed by TMR, not Council — call TMR on 13 20 80 before applying to Council.

Water or sewer infrastructure. If your driveway will pass over, or within 2m of, any Council water main, sewer main, or manhole, you'll also need a separate Works Near Water Supply or Sewerage Infrastructure approval under Section 192(2) of the Water Supply (Safety and Reliability) Act 2008. This is a second form, a second assessment, and a second fee. Council's Engineering Department will identify during your initial enquiry whether this applies.

Most licensed driveway contractors will handle the approval as part of their quote — but ask before signing rather than assuming. Apply early: the Works Within Road Reserve approval is often a condition of building approval, so it pays to lodge alongside (or before) your building application. Call Council on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the Engineering Department for pre-application advice.

faqs.q: Can I request a copy of my building plans or documents relating to past development applications?
faqs.a:
Yes. Council acts as an archival service for all building plans within the Southern Downs region — useful for owners who want to renovate, extend, or simply hold a copy of the original plans for the property.

How to request a copy: email sdrcbuilding@sdrc.qld.gov.au with details of the plans you're after (property address, owner name, approximate year of construction or approval if known, and what you need — for example, decision notice, certificate, floor plans). Council's Building team will get back to you directly to confirm what's available, talk through your options, and arrange payment.

Fee: $68.00 per document (a Decision Notice, Certificate, or set of Plans each count as one document). Council issues plans with accompanying information outlining how the plans can be used, including copyright conditions.

The same process applies whether you're the current owner, a recent purchaser, or a builder working on the property. For older records, The Building Team can advise what's been preserved in the archive — most records are available, but availability varies for very old buildings.

faqs.q: What is a Form 15, Form 16, and Form 21?
faqs.a:
These are standard certificates used throughout the Queensland building process. You'll see them mentioned constantly:

Form 15 — Compliance Certificate for Building Design or Specification. Signed by an RPEQ (registered engineer) to confirm that part of the design meets code. Commonly provided for footings, slabs, and steel framing. Required before building approval can be issued.
Form 16 — Inspection Certificate / Aspect Certificate. Signed by the building certifier (or another competent person) after each stage of construction to confirm that stage passes. Generally you'll collect four of these over the build — footing, slab, frame, final.
Form 21 — Final Inspection Certificate. Issued by the certifier once the final inspection passes and all conditions of approval are met. It's the document that says the building is complete and lawful. For new dwellings, you cannot move in until Form 21 is issued.

Your certifier manages all of these. Keep copies — they're important when you sell the house or change insurance.

faqs.q: What inspections happen during construction?
faqs.a:
For a Class 1a dwelling, the certifier must inspect and sign off at four stages. Each stage must pass before the next commences:

  1. Footing / Foundation — before concrete is poured. Confirms excavation depth, reinforcement, and placement match the engineer's design.
  2. Slab — after slab prep, before the pour. Confirms reinforcement, plumbing penetrations, and setout. Note that removal homes on footings typically skip this stage. 
  3. Frame — once framing (walls, roof structure) is up and before sheeting goes on. Confirms tie-down, bracing, and member sizes. This is often where problems are caught.
  4. Final — at completion. Everything: stairs, balustrades, smoke alarms, waterproofing, energy efficiency, safety, and all conditions of approval.

Your builder arranges inspections directly with your certifier. Plumbing has its own separate inspection schedule managed by Council plumbing inspectors — your plumber handles those bookings.

If a stage fails, the certifier issues a written notice of what needs to be rectified. The work must be corrected and re-inspected before construction continues. If a licensed builder refuses to rectify defective work, the QBCC can issue a formal Direction to Rectify — see the QBCC.

faqs.q: When can I actually move in?
faqs.a:
For a new dwelling, you can move in once the Form 21 Final Certificate has been issued. Not before — even if the house feels finished.

The Form 21 is only issued after the final inspection passes and all conditions of approval are satisfied. Common last-minute holdups: smoke alarm interconnection, balustrade compliance on decks over 1m, final stormwater discharge, and landscaping required by approval conditions.

Occupying a new dwelling before Form 21 is an offence under the Building Act 1975. It can also affect your insurance.

faqs.q: Can I live on the land in a caravan or shed while I build?
faqs.a:
On rural land, yes — but only with Council approval, and only after you've received building approval for the permanent dwelling. It is not automatic, and it is not allowed in urban residential areas.

The process:

  1. Obtain building approval for the dwelling first.
  2. Complete an Application for Permission to Occupy Temporary Accommodation and submit it to Council at least 30 days before your intended start date.
  3. Pay the applicable fee.
  4. Supply supporting information: drawings of the proposed temporary home, wastewater disposal plan, drinking water supply (minimum 5,000L tank required), landowner consent if you're not the owner, and a clear reason for needing temporary occupation.

Approval can be issued for up to 18 months, and Council may extend it to match the expected completion of the permanent dwelling. The temporary accommodation approval lapses automatically once the dwelling is finished, the building approval lapses, or the approval term ends.

Tents and camper trailers are not considered suitable temporary homes. A shed (Class 10a with prior building approval), caravan, or mobile home is. Full detail: SDRC — Temporary Homes.

Don't start living on site before approval is granted. It can void the temporary approval entirely and create enforcement issues.

faqs.q: How do I arrange rubbish collection once I've moved in?
faqs.a:
Kerbside collection in the Southern Downs is contracted to Cleanaway. To start a residential service on a new dwelling, Cleanaway requires a Form 21 Final Certificate as proof the dwelling is complete and lawfully occupied. Until Form 21 is issued, a new property can't be added to the collection round.

The garbage truck doesn't go everywhere. Many rural properties fall outside the Designated Waste Collection Area, so kerbside pickup isn't available. In those areas, Council operates rural bin compounds — shared, gated facilities where ratepayers can drop off their own waste. Residents living in a compound catchment can apply to Council for a key. Call 1300 697 372 to check whether your property is in a compound catchment and to request a key.

Private collection. If your property is outside both kerbside coverage and a bin compound catchment, several private waste operators service rural properties in the region. Ask around locally, or call Council for a starting point.

faqs.q: Where do I get water if my tanks run low?
faqs.a:
Many bulk water carting businesses operate across the Southern Downs region and can deliver to rural tanks. Council maintains a list of approved water carters on the Approved Water Carters page.

If you're arranging a delivery and want to confirm that a carter is licensed and approved to draw from Council's filling stations, call SDRC on 1300 697 372 and staff can confirm approval status.

Planning your water storage from the start saves money on carting over time. Rural dwellings are required to have on-site storage of 45,000L for 1–2 bedrooms, 67,500L for more — these minimums exist to get you through a normal dry spell without needing deliveries.

faqs.q: What costs and fees should I budget for beyond construction?
faqs.a:
Beyond the construction itself, these are the items to keep in mind when budgeting for a new rural home. For current dollar figures, request quotes from the relevant providers and check the current SDRC Fees & Charges schedule.

  • Council building application fee — refer to the current SDRC Fees & Charges.
  • Private certifier fee, if using one.
  • Engineer (RPEQ) — for footing/slab design and Form 15, plus soil test.
  • Energy efficiency assessment — required for all new dwellings.
  • BAL assessment — only if in the Bushfire Hazard Overlay.
  • QBCC Home Warranty Insurance — required for residential work over $3,300. Paid by the builder and added to the contract price.
  • QLeave levy — required for work over $150,000 (excl. GST). Must be paid before building approval is issued.
  • Planning application fee — only if your site needs an MCU. Separate from building fees.
  • Pre-lodgement meeting — optional, $300 for up to 1 hour with Council planners for tailored advice.
  • Infrastructure costs — rural sites often need driveway construction, stormwater management, on-site water storage (45,000L for 1–2 bedrooms, 67,500L for more), and on-site sewage treatment. Get quotes early.

faqs.q: Do I need approval to build on my urban block?
faqs.a:
Almost always yes. Any new dwelling, extension, carport, shed, deck, pool, or retaining wall over 1m needs building approval. Depending on what you're building and where, you may also need planning approval (the two are different — see the next question).

A small number of minor structures are accepted development (self-assessable) under Schedule 2 of the Queensland Building Regulation 2021 — garden sheds under 10m², fences under 2m, and retaining walls under 1m. You still have to comply with the Building Code of Australia, boundary setbacks, and the Planning Scheme, but no permit is needed.

Don't rely on a summary for your specific project. Exact dimensions, location on the lot, and overlays all matter. If in doubt, call 1300 697 372 before spending money.

Reference: Building Regulation 2021 — Schedule 2.

faqs.q: What's the difference between building approval and planning approval?
faqs.a:
Two different questions answered by two different approvals:

  • Planning approval asks: can this use happen on this land? It's about where the building goes, how it's sited, and whether the use fits the Planning Scheme. On an urban block, planning is usually triggered by setback concessions, dual occupancy or secondary dwellings, or building in an overlay (flood hazard, heritage, character).
  • Building approval asks: is the structure itself safe and compliant? It's about how the building is constructed — footings, framing, bracing, tie-down, energy efficiency, smoke alarms.

Most straightforward urban dwellings on standard residential blocks only need building approval — the setbacks and siting fall inside the Planning Scheme's acceptable outcomes, so no planning application is required.

If you want to build closer to a boundary than the standard setback allows, add a second dwelling, or the site has an overlay, you may need planning approval first — and then building approval.

faqs.q: How do I check if my block has any constraints?
faqs.a:
Open the SDRC Online Mapping tool, search your address, and switch on the Planning module. This confirms your zone and shows any overlays — the most common ones in town are:

  • Flood hazard — affects minimum floor levels and may trigger engineering assessment
  • Bushfire hazard — less common in the centres of Warwick and Stanthorpe, more common on the fringes and in smaller townships; may require a BAL (Bushfire Attack Level) report
  • Heritage or character — applies to some older parts of Warwick and Stanthorpe; may add design and materials requirements
  • Airport environs — height restrictions near the Warwick airport
  • Easements — sewer mains, water mains, and drainage easements commonly cross urban blocks and restrict where buildings can go. Check before siting.

Each overlay triggers extra requirements. For specific advice on your block, call the duty planner on 1300 697 372 — general enquiries are free.

faqs.q: Where do I start?
faqs.a:
Here's a short protocol for your first week:

  1. Check your zone and overlays on the Online Mapping tool. Most standard urban blocks fall within the Planning Scheme's acceptable outcomes, but overlays (flood, bushfire, heritage, character) will add requirements.
  2. If anything comes up that isn't straightforward — setback concessions, secondary dwelling, overlay-affected block — call Council on 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner (general enquiries are free). Have your address and a rough description of what you want to build ready.
  3. Based on that call, you will know whether your build fits within the acceptable outcomes or whether planning approval is required. If planning approval is needed and you're not using a private planning consultant, consider booking a Pre-Lodgement Meeting with Council's Town Planners.
  4. Get 2–3 quotes from licensed builders to establish a rough idea of what kind of build is possible within your budget and to get an idea of the possible timeline. If going that route, this is a good time to engage a private certifier.
  5. If you're not using a private certifier, consider booking a Pre-Lodgement Meeting with Council's building certifier to assist with preparing your building application and to discuss the necessary standards for your build to pass inspection when construction begins.

At every step, Council staff are happy to help you understand the process — it's not a test, and you don't have to know all the terminology before you ring. That's what the duty planner is there for.

faqs.q: What are the setback requirements?
faqs.a:
Urban setbacks under the Queensland Development Code differ based on lot size:

Lot size Class 1a (dwellings) Class 10a (sheds, garages, carports)
450m² and over
(QDC MP 1.2)		 6m from front boundary, 1.5m from side & rear boundaries (or a siting concession is required) 1.5m from side & rear boundaries, subject to the QDC MP 1.2 A2(d) exemptions below for smaller outbuildings.
Under 450m²
(QDC MP 1.1)		 Smaller front and side setbacks apply, scaled to the lot. Refer to the Queensland Housing Code for specific numbers. Scaled to lot — refer to QDC MP 1.1 / Queensland Housing Code, or call Council's building team.

Common exemptions for lots 450m² and over under QDC MP 1.2:

  • QDC MP 1.2 A1(c) — Open Carports may be within the road setback if the perimeter of walls, solid screens, and supports within the setback is no more than 15% of the total, and there is no alternative on-site location that complies with normal setbacks, allows vehicle access at least 2.5m wide, and has a maximum gradient of 1 in 5.
  • QDC MP 1.2 A2(d) — Class 10a buildings (sheds, garages, carports) may be within side and rear boundary clearances where height is no more than 4.5m (or mean height no more than 3.5m), the total length of all buildings along any one boundary is no more than 9m, and they are no closer than 1.5m to a window in a habitable room of an adjoining dwelling.

If your design can't meet standard setbacks and doesn't fit an exemption, a siting concession can be requested as part of your building application. The certifier assesses against the QDC's performance criteria, typically considering impact on streetscape, overshadowing, and privacy. A siting concession application adds time and cost to the process.

faqs.q: Should I use a private certifier or Council for building approval?
faqs.a:
Building certifier: a QBCC-licensed professional who checks the building work against the Building Act 1975, the National Construction Code, the Queensland Development Code, and the relevant Australian Standards. They decide the application, arrange inspections, and issue the Form 21 Final Certificate at the end. You can hire a private certifier or use Council as your certifier — the choice is yours.

Council as certifier: available for dwellings and extensions. You prepare and lodge the application yourself (or with your builder's help). Council handles the assessment and inspections. Usually cheaper overall, but more work for you.

Private certifier: the common route for urban dwellings and larger projects. The certifier prepares and lodges the application for you, subcontracts extra professionals as needed (engineers, surveyors, soil tests, energy efficiency report), liaises with Council on your behalf, and conducts on-site inspections. Council fees are the same either way — the certifier charges their own professional fee on top.

Many people find a private certifier is worth the fee — they can catch missing documents before lodgement and optimise the construction schedule to the certification process. As the applicant, it is your decision what will work best for you.

faqs.q: What documents do I need to lodge a building application?
faqs.a:
For a Class 1a dwelling (new house or extension), the full lodgement package is:

  • Completed DA Form 2 (the Qld Government building development application form)
  • Site Plan, Floor Plan, Elevations, and Structural Details
  • Footing / Slab Design with Form 15 signed by a Registered Professional Engineer of Queensland (RPEQ)
  • Soil Test Report
  • Energy Efficiency Report (houses must meet the current energy standard (7-Star))
  • BAL (Bushfire Attack Level) Report — only if the site is in the Bushfire Hazard Overlay
  • QBCC Insurance Certificate if using a licensed builder and the work is $3,300 or more; or QBCC Owner Builder Permit if building yourself and the work is $11,000 or more
  • QLeave payment receipt if the build is valued at $150,000 or more (excl. GST)

Urban sites typically need fewer overlay-specific reports than rural — most blocks don't require a BAL report, bushfire protection measures, or extensive site-specific engineering beyond what's standard. Council's Building Info Sheets list the full requirements.

You cannot commence any building work until you have received the Decision Notice (Approval). Starting early creates unapproved work that has to be undone or retrospectively certified at your cost.

faqs.q: What about extensions, decks, sheds, and carports?
faqs.a:
Rules of thumb for common urban projects (always confirm your specific project with a certifier):

  • Extensions — always need building approval. If the extension pushes into a setback, planning approval or a siting concession is also needed.
  • Decks and patios attached to the dwelling — need building approval. Decks higher than 1m above natural ground level need balustrades compliant with the Building Code.
  • Sheds over 10m² — need building approval. Sheds under 10m² are self-assessable but still have to meet siting rules.
  • Carports — need building approval. Open carports can sometimes sit within the front setback under QDC MP 1.2 A1(c) — see the setback question above.
  • Retaining walls over 1m high — need building approval, with engineering design and Form 15.
  • Fences over 2m — need building approval. Pool fencing has its own separate requirements — see the pool question below.

For a quick yes/no on whether your specific project needs approval, call 1300 697 372.

faqs.q: Do I need approval for my driveway?
faqs.a:
Yes — almost certainly. Any new or upgraded driveway has to cross Council land (the road reserve, including the footpath and verge) to reach the road, and Section 75(2) of the Local Government Act prohibits carrying out works on a road without Council's permission. That permission is called a Works Within Road Reserve approval. It's separate from, and in addition to, your building approval.

Road reserve: the full width of land set aside for a road, including the sealed surface, kerb and channel, footpath, and verge. It's all Council-managed land, even though the footpath and verge may look like part of your front garden.

When you need a Works Within Road Reserve approval:

  • New driveway access (part of virtually every new build)
  • Widening or relocating an existing driveway
  • Changing the surface type (e.g. gravel to concrete)
  • Adding a second access point or a new kerb crossing

Simple resealing or maintenance of an existing surface doesn't normally trigger an approval.

What's involved:

  • Complete the Application for Minor Works — Works Within a Road Reserve form from Council's Engineering Department
  • Attach a sketch plan showing proposed location, dimensions, and any drainage
  • Pay the application fee — see the current Fees & Charges schedule
  • Allow 20 working days for assessment
  • On approval, Council issues an Approval Letter setting out the conditions under which work can proceed

Watch for water and sewer infrastructure. On urban blocks, water mains, sewer mains, and manholes often run under footpaths and front yards. If your driveway will pass over, or within 2m of, any Council water or sewer infrastructure, you'll need a separate Works Near Water Supply or Sewerage Infrastructure approval under Section 192(2) of the Water Supply (Safety and Reliability) Act 2008 — a second form, a second assessment, and a second fee. Telltale signs of infrastructure below include meter boxes, sewer manholes, and valve or hydrant surface boxes on or near the verge. Council's Engineering Department will confirm what applies during your initial enquiry.

Most licensed driveway contractors will handle both approvals as part of their quote — but ask before signing rather than assuming. Call Council's Engineering Department on 1300 697 372 for pre-application advice before any concrete is poured.

faqs.q: What about swimming pools?
faqs.a:
Any pool capable of holding water deeper than 300mm requires both building approval and compliant pool fencing. This includes permanent and most portable/inflatable pools, spas, and portable wading pools that meet the depth threshold.

Pool safety in Queensland is governed by the Building Act 1975 and the Queensland Pool Safety Standard. Key points:

  • The pool must be registered on the Queensland Pool Safety Register.
  • A Pool Safety Certificate is required before selling or leasing a property with a pool, and whenever the fence is replaced or modified.
  • Pool fence inspections are performed by a licensed Pool Safety Inspector, not Council.
  • Council can investigate non-compliant or unfenced pools as a safety matter.

Full guidance, including pool fence specifications, non-compliance reporting, and registration: Swimming Pools — SDRC.

Child drownings are one of the leading causes of accidental death for Queensland children under 5. Pool fencing requirements are strictly enforced and there's no discretion on the standard.

faqs.q: Can I build a granny flat or secondary dwelling?
faqs.a:
The Planning Scheme rules for secondary dwellings are currently being reviewed and may change. Please call Council on 1300 697 372 and speak with the duty planner before committing to a design or contract. General advice is confirmed below, but specific conditions will depend on the current scheme at the time you lodge.

A secondary dwelling (often called a granny flat) is a second, smaller self-contained dwelling on the same lot as an existing house. In urban and rural residential zones, secondary dwellings generally require planning approval (MCU), plus building approval.

General things the scheme looks at:

  • Lot size — larger lots have more flexibility
  • Floor area of the secondary dwelling relative to the main dwelling
  • Separation or attachment to the main dwelling
  • Car parking provision
  • Whether the secondary dwelling can be sold separately (usually not — it remains on the same title)

A dual occupancy (duplex) is different — two dwellings on one lot designed to be equal, often intended for separate titling through a future subdivision. Dual occupancies in urban zones always need planning approval. See the Dual Occupancy checklist for the current rules.

faqs.q: Can I request a copy of my building plans?
faqs.a:
Yes. Council acts as an archival service for all building plans within the Southern Downs region — useful for owners who want to renovate, extend, or simply hold a copy of the original plans for the property.

How to request a copy: email sdrcbuilding@sdrc.qld.gov.au with details of the plans you're after (property address, owner name, approximate year of construction or approval if known, and what you need — for example, decision notice, certificate, floor plans). Council's Building team will get back to you directly to confirm what's available, talk through your options, and arrange payment.

Fee: $68.00 per document (a Decision Notice, Certificate, or set of Plans each counts as one document). Council issues plans with accompanying information outlining how the plans can be used, including copyright conditions.

The same process applies whether you're the current owner, a recent purchaser, or a builder working on the property. For older records, Building can advise what's been preserved in the archive — most records are available, but availability varies for very old buildings.

faqs.q: What is a Form 15, Form 16, and Form 21?
faqs.a:
These are standard certificates used throughout the Queensland building process:

Form 15 — Compliance Certificate for Building Design or Specification. Signed by an RPEQ (registered engineer) to confirm that part of the design meets code. Commonly provided for footings, slabs, and steel framing. Required before building approval can be issued.
Form 16 — Inspection Certificate / Aspect Certificate. Signed by the building certifier (or another competent person) after each stage of construction to confirm that stage passes. You'll collect four of these over the build — footing, slab, frame, final.
Form 21 — Final Inspection Certificate. Issued by the certifier once the final inspection passes and all conditions of approval are met. It's the document that says the building is complete and lawful. For new dwellings, you cannot move in until Form 21 is issued.

Your certifier manages all of these. Keep copies — they're important when you sell the house or change insurance.

faqs.q: What inspections happen during construction?
faqs.a:
For a Class 1a dwelling, the certifier must inspect and sign off at four stages. Each must pass before the next commences:

  1. Footing / Foundation — before concrete is poured.
  2. Slab — after slab prep, before the pour.
  3. Frame — once framing is up and before sheeting goes on.
  4. Final — at completion, including stairs, balustrades, smoke alarms, waterproofing, and all conditions of approval.

Your builder arranges inspections with your certifier. Plumbing inspections are a separate schedule managed by Council plumbing inspectors. If a stage fails, the certifier issues a written notice of what needs to be rectified before construction continues.

faqs.q: When can I move in?
faqs.a:
For a new dwelling, once the Form 21 Final Certificate has been issued. Not before — even if the house looks finished.

The Form 21 is only issued after the final inspection passes and all conditions of approval are satisfied. Common last-minute holdups: smoke alarm interconnection, balustrade compliance on decks over 1m, final stormwater discharge, and any landscaping required by approval conditions.

Occupying a new dwelling before Form 21 is an offence under the Building Act 1975, and can affect your insurance.

Once Form 21 is issued, you can also begin kerbside bin collection — see the Waste & Recycling FAQ for how to arrange.

faqs.q: What is a removal home, and how is the approval different from building new?
faqs.a:
A removal home (or removal dwelling) is an existing house relocated to your land — or moved to a different position on the same land. Both need a building approval, and the building permit for a removal dwelling is valid for 12 months. Depending on the zoning of the land, a planning approval may also be necessary before a building permit can be issued.

The big difference from a new build is Council's extra role as a Concurrence Agency under the Planning Regulation 2017. Because a relocated house can affect the look and amenity of an area, Council assesses its condition and appearance, attaches conditions to the approval, and sets a security bond that must be paid before the house is approved for relocation. The bond is your guarantee that the house will be restored to an acceptable standard once it lands.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council info sheets and a January 2026 referral agency response

faqs.q: What should I check before buying a removal home?
faqs.a:
Two things catch people out, so look at them before you hand over money:

1. The condition report. Your application must include a report by a Registered Professional Engineer of Queensland (RPEQ) or a Building Certifier on the condition of the house against National Construction Code (NCC) requirements. It has to cover the structural adequacy of the house in its new location, the upgrades needed to bring it to current standards — tie down, bracing and strengthening to AS 1684.2 — plus the condition of wet areas, external paint, roof sheeting, and any deteriorated or termite-affected timber. Getting this report done early tells you what the house will really cost.

2. Asbestos. If the structure contains asbestos or asbestos-containing material, an exemption must be obtained under Section 419 of the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (administered by Workplace Health and Safety Queensland) before relocation, and all conditions imposed by the regulator complied with in full.

Asbestos cement roofing must be removed and properly disposed of before the building enters the Southern Downs region.

You'll also need recent photos of the house — every elevation and every internal room — clearly showing the condition of walls, roof sheeting and so on. If the seller can't provide access for the report and photos, treat that as a red flag.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council info sheets and a January 2026 referral agency response

faqs.q: What applications do I need to lodge, and what goes in them?
faqs.a:
You lodge two applications, and both can be emailed to sdrcbuilding@sdrc.qld.gov.au or lodged over the counter at one of Council's Administration Centres. (For email lodgements, a Customer Service Officer will contact you for payment of the applicable fee; over the counter, the fee is payable at lodgement.)

The building approval application should include:

  • Completed DA Form 2
  • Site plan, floor plan, elevations & structural details
  • Footing/slab design and Form 15 (signed by an RPEQ registered engineer)
  • Energy Efficiency Report
  • Bushfire Attack Level Report (if in a Bushfire Prone Zone)
  • Soil Test Report
  • QBCC Insurance Certificate (when a builder/removalist is involved and the value of work is $3,300 or more) or QBCC Owner Builder Permit (when building yourself and the value of work is $11,000 or more)
  • QLeave payment receipt (when the building work value is $150,000 or more, excluding GST)

The amenity and aesthetics (concurrence agency) application should include:

  • Completed Application to Concurrence Agency (Removal Dwelling – Amenity & Aesthetics)
  • The engineer's or certifier's condition report described above
  • Recent photos of all elevations and all internal rooms
Applications may be rejected if any required item is missing — the Building Info Sheets set out the full requirements, so it's worth double-checking before you lodge.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council info sheets and a January 2026 referral agency response

faqs.q: How long does assessment take, and when can work start?
faqs.a:
Building approvals for removal dwellings are code assessable and are assessed in accordance with the timelines in the Development Assessment Rules. If more information is needed, an Information Request is issued to the applicant listed on the DA Form 2. Once all required information has been supplied, a Decision Notice is issued within 35 business days.

After assessment, Council provides written advice of any conditions and the bond amount. Once the bond is paid, the Decision Notice is issued and work on the removal process can begin.

No work of any description may commence until a Decision Notice has been issued.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council info sheets and a January 2026 referral agency response

faqs.q: How much is the security bond?
faqs.a:
The bond amount depends on the zoning of the site the house is moving to:

Zone of the new siteSecurity bond
Rural Zone$15,000
Urban or Rural Residential Zone$30,000

Council confirms the exact amount, along with any conditions, in its written Concurrence Agency advice after assessing your application. If you're happy with the conditions and want to proceed, you then arrange payment of the bond.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council info sheets and a January 2026 referral agency response

faqs.q: How do I pay the bond?
faqs.a:
The bond must be paid — and the Bond Agreement signed and returned — before the house is relocated. Payment can be made by:

  • EFT — include the reference number from your bond agreement
  • Bank cheque — made payable to Southern Downs Regional Council
  • Bank guarantee — must be a signed and dated original, have no termination/expiry date, and be unconditional and payable on demand, with a description (i.e. removal bond)
  • Cash (not preferred)
Council does not accept credit card payments or personal cheques for removal building bonds.

The bond form must be completed in full and accompany your payment. Note that the bond will only be released to the original payee shown on the receipt, so think about whose name it goes in.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council info sheets and a January 2026 referral agency response

faqs.q: How and when do I get the bond back?
faqs.a:
The bond exists to make sure the house is restored to an acceptable standard, so it comes back as the work gets done:

  • Partial refunds may be released progressively at Council's discretion, depending on how much work is complete. They're considered case by case, and up to 50% of the bond is always retained until final release. Bank guarantees can't be released in part — only on completion of all works.
  • Final release happens only once the Final Certificate (Form 21) has been issued after inspection.

Fees apply to refund requests:

RequestFee
Partial refund — inspection required$473.00
Partial refund — no inspection required$237.00
Final release where work isn't completed within 12 months of approval$473.00

To request a refund, send Council a formal request with supporting documents — for a partial release: copies of relevant certificates (including Form 12/Form 16) for the completed work, photos of the completed stages, a schedule of remaining works, and the amount requested. For final release: a copy of the Form 21 from your Building Certifier. Once Council confirms the request is approved, complete a 'Refund or Transfer Payment Request Form – General' (available from Council's financial forms page) and email it to mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au. The requestor must be the party that originally paid the bond, and include your application number and 'full/partial refund of removal bond' as the reason.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council info sheets and a January 2026 referral agency response

faqs.q: Who arranges the transport permits for moving the house?
faqs.a: Your removalist does — it's their responsibility. Before the building can be moved, the removalist must obtain a permit from the Police, and that permit requires approval from both the Department of Transport and Main Roads and Council's Engineering Services. You don't need to arrange these yourself, but it's sensible to confirm your removalist has them in hand before moving day.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council info sheets and a January 2026 referral agency response

faqs.q: What conditions does Council typically put on a removal home approval?
faqs.a:
Conditions are set per application, on a case-by-case basis. Below gives picture of the kind of conditions to expect:

  • A building development application lodged and approved by a building certifier
  • A plumbing and drainage application submitted to Council under the Plumbing and Drainage Act
  • The security bond paid and Bond Agreement signed before the building is relocated
  • The base of the dwelling enclosed with timber battens or other approved materials (batten spacing no more than 50% of the batten width, 75mm from ground)
  • The exterior repainted so the paintwork protects the building materials from weather
  • All defective or deteriorated materials replaced, repaired or made good — commonly the roof sheeting, roof battens, guttering and downpipes, damaged glazing and joinery, barge and fascia boards, eaves soffits, weatherboards (so the building is weatherproof), verandah flooring and stairs
  • Other conditions dependent on the specifics of your chosen structure.  
If you disagree with a condition, you can ask your Building Certifier (the Assessment Manager) to pause the decision for up to 3 months and make written representations to Council — the request to the certifier should be made within 10 business days of the response letter, and your representations within the 3-month period. To discuss a response, contact Council's Planning and Development Department on 1300 697 372.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council info sheets and a January 2026 referral agency response

faqs.q: What inspections happen once the house is on site — and when can I move in?
faqs.a:
Once the house has been relocated, the work must be completed in accordance with the Decision Notice conditions, and these stages must be inspected by the Building Certifier:

  • Footings — before pouring concrete
  • Tie down — preferably while the roof is open and wall frames are exposed
  • Final

When the build passes its final inspection, a Form 21 Final Certificate is issued and arrangements are made to refund the bond.

The dwelling may not be inhabited until the Form 21 has been issued — moving in early is the same rule (and the same risk) as any other new build.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council info sheets and a January 2026 referral agency response

faqs.q: What is town planning, and do I need planning approval?
faqs.a:
Town planning manages how land is used to create functional, sustainable communities — guiding growth, protecting the environment, and making sure people have access to services like water, waste and roads. In practical terms, it's the framework that decides what can be built where, and what has to be assessed before it's built.

Under Queensland's planning system, every development proposal falls into one of three categories:

  • Prohibited — not permitted under any circumstances. Only the state government can designate development as prohibited, and it's rare.
  • Accepted — can proceed without any planning approval. A straightforward new dwelling on a rural block that meets every acceptable outcome in the Planning Scheme is a common example.
  • Assessable — requires planning approval from Council before it can proceed. Most development that doesn't fit neatly inside the acceptable outcomes falls here.
Important: "Assessable" is not the same as "Prohibited." Most things that aren't automatically Accepted are Assessable — meaning they can be approved, just not without going through a formal planning application. If someone tells you, "the Scheme doesn't allow it as Accepted development," that's not a refusal — it's a pathway.

Within Assessable, there are two further pathways:

  • Code Assessment — the application is assessed against the specific codes in the Planning Scheme that apply to your proposal. No public notification is required, and most are decided by a Council planner under delegated authority.
  • Impact Assessment — applies to proposals that may have wider impacts on adjoining land or the surrounding area. Requires public notification, and applications that receive objecting submissions go to a full Council meeting for decision.

The Planning Scheme determines which pathway applies. To see how your specific application would be assessed, view the relevant codes on the Planning Scheme Codes page. The Code vs Impact question further down this page goes into more detail on what each pathway means in practice.

"Do I need planning approval?" is the single most common question the planning team gets. For most property-owner questions, the fastest path to a reliable answer is:

  1. Check your zone and overlays on the Online Mapping tool.
  2. Work through the relevant checklist/factsheet — Council publishes checklists and factsheets for common scenarios (dwellings in the Rural Zone, dual occupancies in Residential / Rural Residential zones, and others). Links to each are on the Planning Information Sheets page.
  3. If the checklist leaves any ✗ marks, or the situation isn't covered by a checklist, call Council's duty planner on 1300 697 372.

faqs.q: What is the Planning Scheme?
faqs.a:
The Southern Downs Planning Scheme is the master document that sets out how land can be used across the region. It describes each zone (Rural, Residential, Rural Residential, Industry, Centre, and others), the overlays that apply to particular pieces of land (flood hazard, bushfire hazard, heritage, character), and the rules and outcomes a development has to meet to be approved.

Importantly, the Planning Scheme is shaped by the community and the state, not written in isolation by Council:

  • Community feedback — the Planning Scheme is developed and amended through public consultation. Residents, landholders, businesses, farmer groups, and Landcare have the opportunity to make submissions during scheme reviews, and those submissions are considered before the scheme is finalised.
  • State regulators — the scheme must align with Queensland's State Planning Policy and regional plans, which reflect state-level goals around housing supply, agricultural protection, environmental values, and infrastructure delivery. The State Government reviews and approves significant scheme amendments.
  • Council — manages the scheme day-to-day, assesses development applications against it, and leads the review process on behalf of the region.

That tri-party structure is why planning decisions sometimes feel more constrained than Council would prefer, and other times more flexible than the community might expect — neither Council nor residents alone set the rules.

The current scheme and supporting documents are available on Council's Planning & Development page.

The Planning Scheme is changing. A new draft Southern Downs Planning Scheme is currently in development, and community consultation is open now. Have your say — make a submission, attend a session, or read the draft at haveyoursay.sdrc.qld.gov.au/draft-southern-downs-planning-scheme. Decisions on current applications continue to be made under the existing scheme until the new one is formally adopted.

faqs.q: What's the difference between planning approval and building approval?
faqs.a:
These sound similar but answer two different questions:

  • Planning approval asks: can this use happen on this land? It's about where the development goes, how it's sited, and whether the use fits the Planning Scheme. Planning looks at setbacks, road access, mapping overlays (flood, bushfire, etc.), whether the use fits the zone, and the impact on neighbouring properties and the broader area.
  • Building approval asks: is the structure itself safe and compliant? It's about how the building is constructed — footings, framing, bracing, tie-down, energy efficiency, smoke alarms, and all the engineering that makes the building safe.

A useful way to think about the split: Planning deals with the land, Building deals with the structure on it. Two separate teams, two separate processes, two separate sets of forms.

Many straightforward developments only need building approval — because the Planning Scheme's acceptable outcomes already cover them. A new rural house that meets every item on the Rural Zone Checklist, or a standard urban dwelling within standard setbacks on a standard block, can usually proceed directly to building approval without needing a separate planning application.

Planning approval becomes necessary when the proposal doesn't fit the acceptable outcomes — for example, setbacks that can't be met, a use that isn't self-assessable in that zone, such as a second dwelling, or a subdivision. In those cases, planning approval must be obtained before building approval — the building certifier will want to see the planning approval before they can assess the building application.

If you're building a straightforward dwelling, the Building Rural or Building Urban FAQ page probably covers what you need. If your project involves anything beyond a single straightforward dwelling — subdivision, a second dwelling, a change of use, short-term accommodation, or a commercial project — you're in planning territory, and the rest of this page is for you.

faqs.q: What type of planning application do I need?
faqs.a:
Three types of planning application cover almost everything residents in the Southern Downs need to lodge:

Reconfiguration of a Lot (RC): changing lot boundaries. Includes subdivision (creating two or more separate lots, each with its own title), boundary realignment, and creating access easements. If lot lines are changing, it's an RC.
Subdivision: a type of Reconfiguration — specifically, splitting one lot into two or more new lots, each able to be sold separately with its own title. Subdivisions are assessed against the Planning Scheme's minimum lot size, access, and servicing requirements for the relevant zone, and typically require infrastructure works (road, water, stormwater) as conditions of approval.
Material Change of Use (MCU): a planning application for a change in how a property is used. The Planning Act 2016 defines an MCU as (a) the start of a new use, (b) the re-establishment of a use that has been abandoned, or (c) a material increase in the intensity or scale of an existing use. Common Southern Downs examples: starting short-term accommodation (Airbnb-style), approving a house site that can't meet standard setback requirements, some second dwellings (granny flats), and commercial or industrial uses on land not already zoned for them.

Which type applies depends on what you're proposing. A single MCU application might be enough for a new rural house that can't meet setbacks. A subdivision into six lots needs an RC. A rural property being converted into farm-stay accommodation needs an MCU. A development that changes boundaries and changes use needs both an RC and an MCU, often lodged together.

If you're unsure which type applies, describe the proposal to the duty planner on 1300 697 372 and they'll tell you. General enquiries are free.

faqs.q: How do I make a planning application?
faqs.a:
The Queensland planning application process has five main parts. Not every application goes through every part — referral, information request, and public notification are conditional.

To be "properly made," a typical application requires:

  • Cover Letter
  • DA Form 1 — the standard Queensland Government development application form
  • Plans — site plan, floor plans, elevations (can be attained by engaging an architect, surveyor, or similar professional)
  • Owner's Consent (signed) — template available on the Queensland Government forms page
  • Application Fee — once you've determined the application type, the fee is listed on Council's Fees & Charges page

To assist in identifying supporting documentation that may be required for your application, visit the Planning Scheme Codes page.

Application — 10 business days to confirm it's properly made
Referral (if applicable) — 10 business days
Information Request (if applicable) — 10 business days
Public Notification (Impact only) — 15 business days
Decision — 35 business days (less time already elapsed)

Part 1 — Application. Council has 10 business days to confirm your application is properly made. If it is, Council issues an Action Notice and Confirmation Notice. If it isn't (missing documents, missing consent, incorrect fee), the clock doesn't start until the issues are resolved.

Part 2 — Referral. If your proposal triggers state-agency referral, you (the applicant) submit directly to the referral agency, not to Council. The main referral agency is the State Assessment and Referral Agency (SARA). Common triggers include:

  • Land within 25 metres of a state-controlled road (e.g. the New England or Cunningham Highway)
  • Clearing or proximity to regulated/protected vegetation
  • Proposals involving a concurrence Environmentally Relevant Activity (ERA)
  • Land on the Queensland Heritage Register

This list isn't exhaustive. Additional fees may be payable to Council and, separately, to the Referral Agency. SARA has 10 business days to respond.

Part 3 — Information Request. Council has 10 business days from when the referral period ends to issue any information request — additional documents, a traffic impact assessment, engineering reports, or other supporting material. The applicant then has up to 3 months to respond.

Part 4 — Public Notification. For Impact Assessment applications only. The applicant runs the notification process — Council provides the signs, but sign placement on every frontage, a newspaper notice, and written notice to adjoining owners are all the applicant's responsibility. The period runs for a minimum of 15 business days. If submissions objecting to the application are received, Council has 10 business days to consider them and the applicant has a further 10 business days to respond.

Part 5 — Decision. Council has 35 business days to decide the application — reduced by time already elapsed during earlier parts. Most applications are decided by the Planning Department under delegated authority, but impact-assessable applications that received objecting submissions go to a full Council meeting for decision. The applicant can request a deputation at a Committee Information Session (CIS) before the decision meeting.

The clock pauses. When the process is waiting on a State Referral Agency, a planning consultant, a surveyor, an engineer, or the applicant themselves, statutory timeframes pause. If a decision feels slow, it's usually because the application is sitting with someone other than Council waiting on a response or a required document. Check the current status via the Application Tracking Tool before assuming Council is the holdup.

Once decided, the applicant receives a Decision Notice. A 20-business-day appeal period follows, during which the applicant can either:

  • Request a Negotiated Decision — by making "change representations" to Council, asking for specific conditions of approval to be reviewed or amended. This is a useful first step if only certain conditions are problematic.
  • Lodge an appeal in the Planning & Environment Court against the conditions, or against a refusal.

For impact-assessable applications, properly-made submitters have a further 20-business-day appeal period after the applicant's, during which they can appeal an approval decision to the Planning & Environment Court.

Approval currency periods — the approved use must commence within this period, or the approval lapses:

  • MCU (Material Change of Use) — 6 years
  • RC (Reconfiguration of a Lot) — 4 years
  • BA + OPW (Building / Operational Works) — 2 years

Conditions of approval must also be complied with throughout the currency period and beyond. When you're ready to commence the approved use, it's worth contacting Council to arrange a compliance inspection — this confirms conditions have been met and reduces the risk of enforcement action later.

faqs.q: Assessable development — what's the difference between Code Assessment and Impact Assessment?
faqs.a:
Once a proposal is assessable (i.e. planning approval is required), the Planning Scheme determines one of two assessment pathways:

  • Code Assessment is the more straightforward pathway. The application is assessed against the specific codes in the Planning Scheme that apply to the proposal. No public notification is required. Most code-assessable applications are decided by a Council planning officer under delegated authority.
  • Impact Assessment applies to proposals that may have wider impacts on adjoining land uses or the surrounding area. Impact Assessment requires public notification — the applicant must erect signs on every frontage, advertise in the newspaper, and notify adjoining owners. Members of the public can lodge submissions either for or against. If submissions objecting to the application are received, the application goes to a full Council meeting for decision rather than being decided under delegation.

The Planning Scheme determines which pathway applies — it's not a choice the applicant or Council makes at the point of lodgement. Generally speaking, uses that fit within the zone's intent get Code Assessment; uses that sit at the edge of or outside the zone's intent get Impact Assessment.

Your planner or duty planner can confirm which pathway your proposal falls into before you lodge. It's worth knowing up front, because Impact Assessment adds a minimum of 15 business days to the timeline for the public notification period alone, plus the cost of signage and advertising.

faqs.q: General enquiry vs Pre-Lodgement Meeting — which do I need?
faqs.a:
Council offers two ways to talk to the planning team before an application is lodged. The right one depends on how specific your question is.

General Enquiry — free. Best for open-ended questions like "what can I do with this block?", "is this use even possible here?", or "which pathway applies to my idea?". Call 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to the duty planner. Good for:

  • Opportunities and constraints of a specific site
  • Clarifying the location of a proposed building
  • Exploring what a particular piece of land might be able to be used for
  • Understanding terminology or application requirements before you commit

Pre-Lodgement Meeting — $300. Best for applicants with a clear, specific development goal who want tailored advice on this specific proposal before lodging a formal application. The meeting helps the applicant understand the key areas of assessment, the likely conditions, and what supporting documents will be required.

Practical details:

  • Booking: complete the Pre-lodgement Request Form and email it to mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au. A Council officer will contact you with payment details, and the meeting is scheduled once payment is received.
  • Wait time: allow up to four weeks for a pre-lodgement meeting to be scheduled — planning staff need time to review your concept plans and prepare tailored advice. Book early.
  • Duration: typically 30 minutes; capped at 1 hour.
  • Location: online via Microsoft Teams, in person at the Warwick office (Wednesday 2pm or 3pm standard), or in person at Stanthorpe on request. Maximum five people in person; unlimited via Teams.
  • What to bring: a filled-out request form with specific questions listed, property details (address, lot & plan, current use, lot size), proposal description, and a site plan — hand-drawn is fine at this stage, as long as boundaries, existing structures, and distances are clear.
  • After the meeting: Council emails you a meeting record of what was discussed within one week.
The $300 fee is credited back to the application. If you lodge an application within 12 months of the pre-lodgement meeting, under the same Planning Scheme, for the same parcel of land, and for the same type of development, the $300 fee is credited against your application fee. Include a copy of the pre-lodgement receipt with the application to claim the credit. The credit applies once per site/proposal — subsequent pre-lodgement meetings on the same matter don't accumulate.

Heads-up — SARA runs its own parallel track.
