If your proposal has state-interest triggers (see the state-controlled road, vegetation, ERA, or Heritage Register points in the application process question), the State Assessment & Referral Agency (SARA) offers its own pre-lodgement meetings to confirm which state codes apply. Book SARA directly — Toowoomba office on 07 4616 7307 or ToowoombaSARA@dsdilgp.qld.gov.au. For complex rural proposals near highways or regulated vegetation, running a Council pre-lodgement and a SARA pre-lodgement is often worthwhile.

A simple test: if you're still exploring options, a general enquiry is the right starting point. If you've already got a concrete plan and you want to refine it before lodging, book a pre-lodgement meeting.

Pre-lodgement advice is not a commitment to approve. The advice given in a pre-lodgement meeting cannot override Council's legislative responsibilities during formal assessment — including considering submissions from the public, referral agency responses, or matters that come to light during detailed assessment. A pre-lodgement meeting reduces surprises; it doesn't guarantee an outcome.

faqs.q: Can I subdivide my rural land?
faqs.a:
In most cases, no — not easily. In line with State Government Planning Policy, subdivision in the Rural Zone is generally not supported. The Southern Downs Planning Scheme sets minimum lot sizes for rural land that are large enough to preserve productive agricultural units and discourage rural-residential fragmentation. If your land is below the minimum for its rural precinct, subdivision is unlikely to be approved — though not impossible, if an Impact Assessment application can demonstrate sufficient merit.

Minimum lot sizes by rural precinct — each new lot created must meet the minimum for that precinct:

PrecinctMinimum lot size
Alluvial Plains200 hectares (~494 acres)
Basalt Quality Grazing200 hectares (~494 acres)
Basalt Uplands200 hectares (~494 acres)
Granite Belt100 hectares (~247 acres)
Granite Hills500 hectares (~1,235 acres)
Granite Plains500 hectares (~1,235 acres)
Sandstone Rises & Traprock Hills700 hectares (~1,730 acres)
Walloon Arable200 hectares (~494 acres)

Find your planning zone by searching the property on the Online Mapping tool — the planning module shows the zone and gives access to many of the relevant overlays. To identify the specific rural precinct for a rural-zoned property, consult the Rural Zone Precincts Map.

There is no "family" exemption. Council does not grant exceptions for subdivisions intended for a family member — a child building a house, a parent downsizing, or succession planning. All subdivision applications are assessed against the same minimum lot-size requirements regardless of who the new lot is intended for. This comes up often and the answer is consistent.

If you meet the minimum — subdivisions that meet the precinct minimum are typically assessed as Reconfiguration of a Lot (RC) applications against the scheme's standard codes. Council's duty planner can confirm the pathway, and for anything beyond straightforward it's worth engaging a town planner or surveyor.

If you don't meet the minimum — an application is still technically possible, but it will be Impact Assessable and will go to a full Council meeting for decision. The applicant bears the cost of public notification, and the onus is on the applicant to demonstrate why the proposal warrants a departure from the scheme's minimum. These applications are rare and are approved rarely. If you're thinking of going down this path, start with a pre-lodgement meeting ($300, up to 1 hour — see the pre-lodgement question above).

Related — dual occupancies, secondary dwellings, and multiple dwellings. If the goal is more housing on the land rather than separate titles, subdivision isn't the only option. See the second dwelling question below, or discuss options with the duty planner.

faqs.q: Do I need planning approval to build a second dwelling on my land?
faqs.a:
A second dwelling — sometimes called a granny flat, a duplex when attached, or in formal planning terms a dual occupancy — is two dwellings on the one property, whether attached or detached. Whether you need planning approval depends almost entirely on the zone of your land, its size, and its road frontage. Check your planning zone on the Online Mapping tool by searching the property address, then skip to the relevant section below.

If your land is in the Rural zone

On proper rural land, a second dwelling can often proceed without planning approval — but only if all three of the following are true:

  • The lot is at least 10 hectares in area,
  • The lot has frontage to a constructed road (or a constructed road accessed via a registered easement), and
  • The proposal meets the acceptable outcomes set out in the Planning Scheme (watercourse setbacks, flood-free building pad, separation from animal industries and extractive industries, on-site water storage, and so on).

If all three apply, you'll still need building and plumbing approvals, but no planning application is required.

If the lot is at least 10 hectares and has constructed road frontage but the proposal can't meet every acceptable outcome, a code-assessable MCU is needed — assessed against the scheme's performance outcomes rather than refused outright.

If the lot is smaller than 10 hectares, the application is impact-assessable, which means public notification and a decision at an ordinary Council meeting. These are rare, and it's worth a pre-lodgement meeting before committing.

If your land is in the Low Density Residential zone

Planning approval is always required. The question is just which pathway:

  • Code assessable — if the lot is at least 800m².
  • Impact assessable — if the lot is smaller than 800m².

If your land is in the Medium Density Residential zone

Planning approval is always required, and is code assessable regardless of lot size.

If your land is in the Rural Residential zone

  • Code assessable — if the lot is at least 8,000m² and has frontage to a constructed road.
  • Impact assessable — if the lot is smaller than 8,000m² or doesn't have constructed road frontage.

Three or more dwellings is different

Three or more dwellings on one lot — flats, units, townhouses, triplexes — is a Multiple Dwellings development, not a dual occupancy, and the rules are different. In short: only permitted in Low and Medium Density Residential zones, subject to density caps (roughly one dwelling per 500m² in Low Density, or one per 250m² in Medium Density, with slightly more generous ratios for small one-bedroom units). Low Density applications are always impact-assessable; Medium Density is code-assessable. It's a rarer question — call the duty planner on 1300 697 372 to discuss your specific site.

Things to keep in mind regardless of zone

  • Overlays can change the picture. Flood hazard, bushfire hazard, biodiversity, heritage, and Morgan Park / Airport environs overlays can each add requirements. Check the Online Mapping tool.
  • Building, plumbing, and drainage approvals are always required, separate from planning. The Planning Scheme requirements sit on top of the Building Code of Australia, not in place of it.
  • Typical conditions of approval (where planning approval is needed): road works and site access, off-street parking, stormwater discharge, landscaping, buffering from incompatible uses, and infrastructure charges.

Full fact sheets — including the complete acceptable-outcome checklists for each zone — are on the Planning Information Sheets page. For anything that looks borderline, a 10-minute call with the duty planner will save time and money later.

faqs.q: What approval is required to start a business from my home?
faqs.a:
Plenty of small businesses operate legitimately from a home in the Southern Downs without any planning approval at all — online retailers, consultants, tutors, bookkeepers, tradespeople whose work happens at other sites, family day care, bed & breakfasts. The Planning Scheme has a dedicated Home Based Business framework that defines what can happen at home without needing a Material Change of Use, and what tips over into needing one.

Like short-term accommodation, running a business from home is best thought of as a stack of separate approvals — even when planning approval isn't required, other permits often still are. The most common combination:

  1. Planning approval — only required if your business steps outside the Home Based Business framework (see limits below).
  2. Industry-specific licence — required for food businesses and personal appearance services regardless of planning. Detailed below.
  3. Building approval — only if you're physically modifying the building or, in rare cases, changing its building classification (e.g. running guest accommodation on the same property — see the short-term accommodation question below).

If your business fits within all of these, no planning approval is needed:

  • Size of the operation — up to 40m² of the home in residential zones, or up to 100m² in the Rural zone.
  • Staff — in residential zones, only residents of the dwelling. In the Rural zone, residents plus one employee who doesn't live on-site.
  • Clients on site — maximum six at any one time, between 8:00am and 7:00pm Monday to Saturday (excluding public holidays). Family day care has its own rules — see below.
  • Signage — one sign, 0.3m² maximum, showing only the name, occupation, and contact details of the occupier.
  • No retail sales from the premises — mail order and online sales are fine, but no walk-in retail, no goods on public display, no outside storage.
  • Vehicles — one commercial vehicle associated with the business (two in Rural). No vehicle over 4.5 tonnes in residential zones. No fuelling, repairing, or maintenance (beyond cleaning) of vehicles on site.
  • Not a motor vehicle workshop, medium-impact industry, or high-impact industry — these are never home-based business, regardless of scale.

Family day care fits inside the Home Based Business framework with one specific rule: the maximum number of children being minded at any one time is six (children under school age, in a family day care environment). Other limits in the list above continue to apply.

Looking at running a B&B or Airbnb-style let? See the short-term accommodation questions below — the approvals required are different (and there are more of them).

If your business steps outside any of those limits, it's treated as a Material Change of Use (MCU) — which means a planning application. This is more common than people assume, and it doesn't mean Council will refuse it. An MCU is simply the pathway that lets Council assess the proposal against the Planning Scheme's Performance Outcomes rather than the strict Acceptable Outcomes. Plenty of home-based operations that don't fit the default ratios get approved with conditions around hours, parking, signage, neighbour notification, and the like. If you think your plan might need an MCU, call the duty planner before you commit to anything — general enquiries are free. A 10-minute conversation can shape a proposal in a way that makes approval straightforward.

Industry-specific Council permits — required regardless of planning:

  • Food businesses — if you prepare or sell food as part of your business (baked goods, meals, catering, market stalls, mobile coffee, home kitchens), a separate Food Business Licence is required under the Food Act 2006. See Food Businesses.
  • Personal Appearance Services — body piercing, tattooing, beauty therapy, and other skin penetration services require a licence under the Public Health (Infection Control for Personal Appearance Services) Act 2003, regardless of the setting. See Personal Appearance Services.

Things that aren't Council's remit but are worth knowing about: you'll likely need an ABN (Australian Business Register), consideration of the tax implications of running a business from home (ATO), a working with children check if your business involves minors (Blue Card Services), a liquor licence if you intend to serve alcohol (Office of Liquor and Gaming Regulation), and WorkCover if you employ staff. These sit outside Council's regulatory remit but are often part of a successful small business launch — Business Queensland (business.qld.gov.au) has good checklists for each.

The full Home Based Business provisions are in section 9.3.4 of the Southern Downs Planning Scheme. For anything that looks borderline, or to discuss whether an MCU is the right path for your specific business, call Council's duty planner on 1300 697 372.

faqs.q: What approvals are required for short-term accommodation?
faqs.a:
Short-term accommodation — Airbnb-style lets, B&Bs, holiday cabins, motels, farm-stays, caravan parks — involves more approvals than people often realise. Best to think of it as a stack of separate approvals, not a single application. Generally three apply, sometimes four:

  1. Planning approval — sometimes required, depending on zone, scale, and number of guests. Often not required for letting an existing house in town to a small number of guests.
  2. Building approval — reclassification of the dwelling from Class 1a to Class 1b — always required when an existing dwelling is used for short-term accommodation, even when no building work is involved.
  3. Local Law permit to Operate Rental Accommodation — always required.
  4. Plumbing & drainage approval — required only if your conversion involves plumbing work.
This change will affect the Rates and Charges applicable to your property. Once a property is reclassified for short-term accommodation, it shifts to a different rates category. Contact Council's Revenue Department for specifics before committing. 

Where to next?

  • Letting an existing house in town for short stays (Airbnb-style)? See "Can I rent out my house for short-term stays in town?" below.
  • Cabins, farm-stay, motel-style accommodation, or a caravan park on rural land? See "Can I run short-term accommodation or a caravan park on rural land?" below.

For anything that looks borderline, or to talk through your specific concept before committing, call the duty planner on 1300 697 372. General enquiries are free.

faqs.q: Can I rent out my house for short-term stays in town? (Airbnb-style)
faqs.a:
Most likely yes — and from a planning perspective the path is the most permissive in the scheme. Check your planning zone on the Online Mapping tool by searching the property address. This question covers properties in the Low Density Residential and Medium Density Residential zones.

Three approvals apply for renting out an existing house — sometimes a fourth. See the framework question above for the full stack; this question covers each of them as they apply specifically in town.

Planning approval — often not required

You generally don't need planning approval if all of the following are true:

  • The accommodation is in an existing dwelling (not a new build, and not a non-dwelling building like a converted shed),
  • A maximum of six guests stay at any one time, and
  • The proposal meets the acceptable outcomes set out in the Planning Scheme (parking, amenity, signage, hours, and similar).

If you can't meet every acceptable outcome, you'll need a code-assessable planning application. If you want to take more than six guests, build a new accommodation building, or use a non-dwelling building, the application becomes impact-assessable — public notification and decision at a Council meeting.

Building approval — reclassification from Class 1a to Class 1b

This catches a lot of operators by surprise. Under the Building Act 1975, an existing house is classified as Class 1a (a dwelling). Once it's used for short-term accommodation, it's no longer a dwelling — it's Class 1b (a small boarding-style building). That reclassification is a separate building approval, and it's required regardless of whether any physical building work is happening. The classification itself triggers requirements designed for paying guests rather than residents:

  • Smoke alarms — interconnected hard-wired alarms, in or near the ceiling, in every bedroom and in every corridor associated with bedrooms.
  • Evacuation lighting — a lighting system activated by the smoke alarm to assist evacuation. Existing artificial lighting can be used if it's wired to activate from the alarm.
  • Balustrades and stairs — required for any landing, verandah, or deck floor more than 1m above ground, complying with current Building Code of Australia standards.
  • Disabled access — required to one bedroom and associated bathroom where there are four or more guest bedrooms, plus access to common-use rooms.
  • Bushfire overlay properties — additional requirements apply per the Development in the Bushfire Hazard Overlay factsheet.

How to lodge:

  • By email to sdrcbuilding@sdrc.qld.gov.au, or in person at one of Council's Administration Centres.
  • Application package: a completed DA Form 2, site plan (north point, existing buildings, distances to boundaries), floor plan (showing smoke alarms, escape lighting, entrance and exit doors), plus a QBCC Insurance Certificate (if a builder is involved and the work is $3,300 or more) or QBCC Owner Builder Permit (if you're doing the work yourself and it's $11,000 or more).
  • Decision is issued within 35 business days of complete information. After Council's certifier inspects and finds the building compliant, a Form 11 Certificate of Occupancy is issued. (Note: this is different from the Form 21 issued for a new dwelling — the Form 11 is the reclassification version.)
  • Once Form 11 is issued, you can apply for the Local Law permit (next step).

Local Law permit to Operate Rental Accommodation

Lodged after the building reclassification is complete, and managed under Council's Local Law. See the Licences & Permits for Business page for the application form and current fee.

Plumbing & drainage approval (if applicable)

If your reclassification involves any new bathrooms, ensuites, additional fixtures, or changes to existing plumbing, a separate plumbing & drainage application is required. If no plumbing work is involved, this approval isn't needed.

Other things worth knowing

  • Food licence — if you serve any food (breakfasts, packaged snacks, mini-bar items prepared on premises), a separate Food Business Licence is required under the Food Act 2006. See the food businesses link in the home business question above.
  • Rates and charges change once the property is reclassified — see the framework question above.

Full fact sheets — including the building reclassification factsheet and acceptable-outcomes checklists — are on the Planning Information Sheets page. For anything that looks borderline, call the duty planner on 1300 697 372.

faqs.q: Can I run short-term accommodation or a caravan park on rural land?
faqs.a:
Yes, but the rural pathway is more involved than the in-town pathway — planning approval is always required in the Rural zone, and the building reclassification, Local Law permit, and other approvals from the framework question above all still apply on top.

Two distinct uses are contemplated on rural land:

  • Short-term accommodation — cabins, farm-stay, motel-style accommodation in buildings.
  • Tourist parks — caravan parks and camping grounds.

Cabins, farm-stay, motel-style accommodation

Two thresholds determine which planning assessment pathway applies:

  • Code assessable — if your lot is at least 5 hectares, you have no more than 2 accommodation buildings, and a maximum of 12 guests at any one time.
  • Code assessable — if your lot is at least 10 hectares, you have no more than 4 accommodation buildings, and a maximum of 24 guests at any one time.
  • Impact assessable — anything outside those two brackets.

Code-assessable applications are decided by a planner under delegated authority and don't require public notification. Impact-assessable applications are decided at a Council meeting and require public notification — they take longer, cost more, and are best discussed with the duty planner before lodging.

Caravan parks and camping grounds (Tourist Parks)

  • Code assessable — if your lot is at least 10 hectares and you have no more than 20 sites.
  • Impact assessable — anything larger or on a smaller lot.

Tourist parks have a separate ongoing layer: Council's Caravan Parks Local Law governs operation once approved, including amenities ratios, dump points, and waste management. The duty planner will steer you toward those requirements early.

The other approvals from the framework question still apply

  • Building approval — required for any new accommodation buildings, and the Class 1a → 1b reclassification still applies if you're using or converting an existing dwelling. See the in-town question above for what the reclassification involves; the same standards apply on rural land, with bushfire overlay considerations more likely to be relevant.
  • Local Law permit to Operate Rental Accommodation — always required.
  • Plumbing & drainage approval — for new bathrooms, amenities blocks, or significant changes to existing plumbing.
  • State environmental approvals may apply for larger sites without reticulated sewerage — common on rural land. The duty planner can flag what's likely to apply.
  • Food licence — separate licence required under the Food Act 2006 if any food is served.

Rates and charges change once a property is reclassified for short-term accommodation — see the framework question above for context.

Rural accommodation often involves bushfire overlays, watercourse setbacks, and on-site sewerage that affect what's possible on a specific block. Strongly recommended: book a Pre-Lodgement Meeting with Council's Town Planners before committing significant money to plans. The fee is small relative to what it can save you in avoided redesign or refusal. Call the duty planner on 1300 697 372 to discuss your specific situation — general enquiries are free.

faqs.q: How do I check on the status of a planning application?
faqs.a:
If you have specific questions about your own application, the planning officer assigned to the file is the best contact — easiest to contact via email, or call 1300 697 372 to be transferred directly. If the officer is unavailable, Customer Service can take your details and arrange a callback.

For applications that aren't yours, the Application Tracking Tool and the Online Mapping tool together cover most of what's publicly available. Some information is withheld from non-applicants for privacy reasons.

Council's Application Tracking Tool is the self-service tool for checking the publicly available information of any planning application in the Southern Downs region. It shows lodgement dates, current stage, and decision status for every application post 2010.

The tracking tool is most commonly used for:

  • A neighbour's application — particularly for housing estates, subdivisions, or commercial developments nearby, where residents want to understand what's being proposed before deciding whether to make a submission
  • Due diligence on a property you're considering buying — checking whether any active or recent applications affect the land

faqs.q: How do I object to a planning application near me?
faqs.a:
Only Impact Assessment applications go through public notification, so submissions can only be made during an active public notification period. If the application is proceeding under Code Assessment, there is no public submission process — Council assesses against the codes without public input.

To make a properly made submission — which ensures your objection is considered in the decision and preserves your right of appeal — the submission must:

  • Be in writing and signed by each person making the submission
  • Be received during the public notification period (usually 15 business days; check the specific dates on the site signage or in the newspaper notice)
  • Include the name and address of every submitter
  • Include one (1) postal or electronic address for all submission-makers
  • Include the grounds of the submission — the facts and circumstances you're relying on in support of those grounds
  • Be addressed to the assessment manager: Southern Downs Regional Council

Grounds that carry weight relate to the Planning Scheme — impacts on traffic, noise, amenity, hours of operation, overshadowing, character of the area, stormwater, environmental values, and similar. Personal or commercial grievances (disliking the applicant, competing with the proposed business, diminution of property value) generally don't carry weight in planning terms — Council has to assess the application against the scheme, not against commercial or personal interests.

If the application is approved despite submissions objecting to it, properly-made submitters have a right of appeal to the Planning & Environment Court. If the application is refused, all submitters are notified and receive a copy of the Decision Notice.

If you're unsure whether an application is code- or impact-assessable, or how to word a submission, call the duty planner on 1300 697 372. Council can't tell you what to say in a submission — that would be inappropriate — but they can clarify the process, timeframes, and what the scheme considers relevant.

faqs.q: I can't find an application in eProperty. What am I doing wrong?
faqs.a:
Usually nothing — it's the search, not you. eProperty rewards a narrower set of fields, not a fuller one.

  • Search by suburb or by application number wherever you can.
  • Avoid searching by full street address. Exact addresses often return nothing even when they are correct.
  • Fill in as few fields as possible. Adding more fields, even accurate ones, reduces the chance of a match rather than improving it.
If a search by suburb returns a long list, sort or scan it rather than adding fields to cut it down. Still stuck? Call 1300 697 372.

faqs.q: How do I register my dog?
faqs.a:
Dog Registration Fees & Forms

Download and complete a Dog Registration Form for dogs over 12 weeks of age.  Discounted fees apply for desexed & microchipped animals, and aged pensioners are also entitled to a reduced fee.  See Fees & Charges schedule for current fees.



  1. All dogs must be registered from 12 weeks of age;
  2. All new animals to the region must be registered within 14 days of arrival;
  3. Microchipping is compulsory for animals from 12 weeks of age; and
  4. Working dogs ONLY will be exempt from mandatory registration and microchipping - See Working Dogs for further information.
  5. Desexing is recommended at an appropriate age



Full details: Dog Registration — SDRC website.

faqs.q: Do I need to register my cat?
faqs.a:
No. Cats don't need to be registered with Council in the Southern Downs. However, microchipping is mandatory for cats over 12 weeks of age under Queensland law (the Animal Management (Cats and Dogs) Act 2008), regardless of whether they're indoor-only.

The number of cats you can keep without a permit depends on where you live — see the next question for the full table. If you breed cats, separate rules apply — see "I'd like to breed cats" further down.

faqs.q: How many animals am I allowed to keep on my property?
faqs.a:
Permitted numbers vary by zone, lot size, and animal type, set by Council's Local Law No. 2 (Animal Management) and the Planning Scheme.

Cats (over the age of three months — kittens under three months don't count toward the limit):

  • Aerodrome precinct (Massie or Applethorpe) — 0 cats (no animals at all permitted in these precincts)
  • Multi-residential premises — 1 cat
  • Designated town area, lot under 2,000m² — 2 cats
  • Designated town area, lot 2,000m² or more — 3 cats
  • Outside designated town areas — 4 cats

Dogs and other animals — limits vary depending on zone, lot size, and animal type. The full breakdown is in the Keeping of Animals Fact Sheet.

To keep more animals than the standard limits, a Permit for Keeping of Animals is required under Subordinate Local Law No. 1.5. Permits are issued for 12 months and require annual renewal. Conditions typically include desexing, no nuisance to neighbours, and a sanitary enclosure. Cat breeders can apply for an Animal Breeder Permit for up to four breeding cats — see the breeding question further down.

Call Council on 1300 697 372 to discuss your situation before applying.

faqs.q: How many animals can I keep on a rural block?
faqs.a:
Rural zoned land generally allows a broader range and number of animals than residential land — horses, cattle, sheep, goats, alpacas, poultry, and similar are all typical. There are still limits, though, and the limits depend on what type of animal, your lot size, and your zone.

The Keeping of Animals Fact Sheet sets out the permitted numbers by animal type and zone. It's the definitive source — everything from dogs and cats, to horses, cattle, poultry, bees, pigs, and exotic animals is covered, with the maximum you can keep without a permit for each.

If you want to keep more than the standard number, you'll need a Keeping of Animals permit. Call Council on 1300 697 372 to discuss your situation before applying — the Local Laws team can advise whether a permit is likely to be approved for your block before you put an application in.

Some breeds and species are restricted or prohibited regardless of lot size (restricted breed dogs, some reptiles, feral animals). Check the fact sheet before buying, breeding, or relocating animals to a new property.

faqs.q: Can I adopt a dog or cat from Council?
faqs.a:
Generally, adoptions are handled by Southern Downs ARK — a local volunteer-run organisation that works with Council to rehome impounded and surrendered animals. ARK takes most animals from the Council pound, gets them vet-checked, vaccinated, microchipped, and desexed, and then matches them with new homes. They're the best first stop if you're looking to adopt.

Visit Southern Downs ARK to view current animals available, adoption fees, and the application process.

In rare cases, if there's a specific animal at the Council pound that you'd like to adopt directly through Council, call 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to a Local Laws Officer. This is uncommon — most adoptions go through ARK — but it's possible if the circumstances suit.

faqs.q: Can I surrender my pet?
faqs.a:
Yes. Council accepts surrendered dogs and cats, although surrendering with Southern Downs ARK directly is often a smoother process for the animal — they can begin the rehoming work immediately rather than the animal going through the pound first. Visit Southern Downs ARK to find out more.

If you choose to surrender to Council:

  • A surrender fee applies — see Council's Fees & Charges page for the current rate.
  • Complete the Owners Request to Privately Impound Dog/Cat form, available from Council's Customer Service Centres or by request through 1300 697 372.
  • You'll need to provide details about the animal (breed, age, colour, microchip number, registration, vaccination status) and the reason for surrender.
  • Council reserves the right to decline surrender, particularly for injured or seriously ill animals — in those cases a vet is the appropriate first contact.

Once surrendered, the animal becomes the responsibility of Council and may be transferred to ARK for rehoming.

If you've come across feral or pest animals on your property — wild dogs, feral cats, foxes, or feral pigs — those aren't surrender situations. See the Pest Animals page for the appropriate management options.

faqs.q: My dog is missing or has been impounded. What do I do?
faqs.a:
Call Council on 1300 697 372 as soon as possible with your dog's breed, colour, size, and tag number. If impounded, a Local Laws Officer will advise the collection time, release fee, and whether registration is required before release. If your dog has not been impounded, we will add your dog's details to our lost and found register to assist with reuniting you with your dog once found. 

You can also check the Impounded and Rescued Animals page.

faqs.q: Where are the Council pound facilities?
faqs.a:
Council operates two pound facilities in the Southern Downs region:

  • Warwick Pound — 113 Wentworth Street, Warwick QLD 4370
  • Stanthorpe Pound — 26270 New England Highway, Stanthorpe QLD 4380

Hours and contact details for each pound are on Council's Pound Facilities page. Before attending, call Council on 1300 697 372 to confirm your animal is at the pound and to arrange payment of any fees as required.

faqs.q: I've found a stray dog. What should I do?
faqs.a: Call Council on 1300 697 372. A Local Laws Officer will attend to collect the animal. Please don't attempt to physically restrain an unknown dog — even a friendly animal can bite when stressed.

faqs.q: There's livestock on the road. Who do I call?
faqs.a:
For animals on Council roads call 1300 697 372. Local Laws Officers attend livestock-on-road incidents as a priority because of the safety risk to motorists. If the animal is on a highway call 13 19 40 to alert TMR who are better equipped to attend highway hazards safely. 


Information to have ready when you call helps the response:

  • The closest street address or landmark — and the direction the animal is travelling
  • Animal type (cattle, horse, sheep, goat) and approximate number
  • Breed or colour if you can identify it
  • Whether the animal appears injured or distressed


If the situation is an immediate hazard — animals on a major road at night, or after a vehicle collision — call 000 first, then notify Council.

faqs.q: I've found injured wildlife, or there's a snake or possum in the house. What do I do?
faqs.a:
Council does not attend wildlife callouts directly — wildlife rescue is handled by specialist volunteer organisations licensed under Queensland's wildlife management framework. Council's role is to provide information and direct you to the right service.

For injured wildlife (kangaroos, koalas, birds, possums hit by vehicles or otherwise injured): see Council's Caring for Wildlife page for current rescue group contacts and what to do while you wait. After an emergency event such as flood, fire, or storm, the Help After a Disaster — Wildlife page is the right starting point.

For snakes and possums in homes: Council's Possums and Snakes page lists licensed snake catchers and possum-removal contacts in the region. Don't attempt to handle a snake yourself — even non-venomous species can deliver painful bites, and a misidentification is dangerous.

faqs.q: My neighbour's dog barks constantly. Can Council do something?
faqs.a:
Yes. Persistent barking is a noise nuisance Council can investigate under local laws. The process works in steps:

  1. Try direct contact first. In many cases the owner isn't aware — a friendly note often resolves it without Council involvement.
  2. Lodge a service request via Council's online service request form or by calling 1300 697 372.
  3. Keep a noise diary. Council will ask you to record dates, times, and how the barking affects you. This is essential — without it, Council has limited ability to take action.
  4. Council investigates. Once the diary is received, a Local Laws Officer will contact the dog owner.
Download the Barking Dogs Fact Sheet and Noise Diary to get started.

faqs.q: Why does Council need a noise diary? Why can't an officer just come and listen?
faqs.a: Upon receiving a noise complaint Local Laws Officers will begin their investigation immediately. However, the barking dog diary creates an objective record showing a pattern — which Local Laws Officers need to demonstrate a genuine nuisance under the legislation. It also protects you by documenting the problem factually.

faqs.q: I've been told my dog barks when I'm away. What are my options?
faqs.a:
Most persistent barking has an underlying cause — boredom, separation anxiety, territorial stress, lack of exercise, or something in the environment the dog is reacting to. Addressing the cause usually works better than trying to suppress the symptom. Practical first steps: more exercise, enrichment toys, a secure and shaded spot to rest, and (where possible) reducing line-of-sight to things that set the dog off.

As a short-term tool for behaviour modification, Council also hires out barking collars to residents. Hire is $15 per week or part thereof, with a $100 refundable deposit. The deposit must be claimed within three months of returning the collar, or it will not be refunded.

How to hire: Complete the Application for Hire of Cat/Fox Trap or Barking Collar or Tree Pear Injector form and submit it — along with proof of identity (driver's licence, passport, or other acceptable ID) — to the Warwick, Stanthorpe, or Allora Customer Service Centre. Prices current as of April 2026 and subject to change — see Council's current Fees & Charges schedule for any updates.

If the barking persists despite reasonable efforts, it's worth speaking with your vet or an animal behaviourist. A medical issue (pain, cognitive decline in older dogs) or severe separation anxiety may need professional attention rather than equipment.

faqs.q: I've been attacked by a dog. What do I do?
faqs.a:
If anyone needs emergency medical attention, call 000 first.

Once you're safe, call Council on 1300 697 372 to record the details of the incident. If necessary, a Local Laws Officer will attend the scene. You will also need to submit a Statement of Dog Attack form — email the completed form to mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au. When you call, have ready: the location, a description of the dog, whether it is still in the area, and the time of the attack.

faqs.q: I'm thinking of breeding my dog. What do I need to do?
faqs.a:
Dog breeding in Queensland is governed by state law — administered by Biosecurity Queensland under the Animal Management (Cats and Dogs) Act 2008. Council's role is supporting the system, not running it.

The headline rule: if you breed a dog (born on or after 26 May 2017), you must register as a breeder with the Queensland Dog Breeder Register and obtain a supply number that gets included in the puppy's microchip information. This applies even if:

  • You're a casual or "mum and dad" breeder
  • The litter was unplanned or accidental
  • You're only giving puppies to family or friends

The narrow exemption is for primary producers on rural land breeding working dogs for other primary producers to use as working dogs (see the next question for the legal definition).

What to do, in order:

  • Register online at the Queensland Dog Breeder Register — registration is free and the process is quick. You'll receive a Breeder Identification Number (your "supply number") that's valid for 12 months and renewable annually.
  • You must register within 28 days of a litter being born.
  • When the puppies are microchipped (mandatory under state law), the implanter must include your supply number in the chip information.
  • When you sell, give away, or advertise a puppy, the supply number must be displayed in the advertisement and provided to the new owner.

Penalties apply for selling or giving away a puppy without a supply number — both for the breeder and for any pet shop or third party that on-sells without proper documentation.

Find-a-stray and one-off scenarios: if you've found a dog you'd like to rehome (rather than surrendering it to Council), or you're a non-business owner rehoming a dog you didn't breed, you may qualify for a Breeder Exemption Number instead. Apply through the same Queensland Dog Breeder Register portal.

Council can't register breeders or issue supply numbers — for those questions, contact Biosecurity Queensland on 13 25 23 or visit qdbr.daf.qld.gov.au.

faqs.q: I'm a primary producer with working dogs. Do the breeder rules apply to me?
faqs.a:
Mostly no, but with important conditions. Working dog breeders are exempt from the registration requirement, but the exemption is narrower than many landholders assume.

Under the Animal Management (Cats and Dogs) Act 2008, a working dog is defined as a dog usually kept (or proposed to be kept) on rural land, by an owner who is a primary producer (or someone employed by a primary producer), primarily for droving, protecting, tending, or working stock — or being trained to do so.

Pig-dogs are explicitly NOT working dogs under the Act. The legal definition is limited to dogs working stock — managing feral animals doesn't qualify.

The exemption applies only when:

  • You are a primary producer breeding on rural land, AND
  • All the puppies are supplied to other primary producers, AND
  • Those puppies will be kept on rural land as working dogs.

If you supply any puppy from the litter for any other purpose — sold to a non-primary-producer, kept as a pet, given to a friend in town — you must register as a breeder for that puppy and provide a supply number.

Selling a working dog you didn't breed to a non-primary-producer or to someone who won't use it as a working dog requires a Breeder Exemption Number for that specific dog, even though you're a primary producer. Apply through the Queensland Dog Breeder Register — a separate exemption number is required for each individual dog.

If in doubt, register. It's free, takes minutes, and avoids penalties.

faqs.q: I'd like to breed cats. What permits do I need?
faqs.a:
Cat breeding sits across both state law (microchipping requirements under the Animal Management (Cats and Dogs) Act 2008) and Council's local laws and Planning Scheme for the keeping of breeding cats.

Up to 4 breeding cats — Animal Breeder Permit (Council)

If you wish to keep more cats than the standard limits (see "How many animals am I allowed to keep" above), you can apply to Council for an Animal Breeder Permit for up to four breeding cats. To apply you'll need:

  • The completed application form
  • Plans and details of the cats' enclosure
  • The application fee (see Fees & Charges)
  • Written evidence of affiliation with a recognised cat breeder association, and registration of all breeding cats with that association

More than 4 breeding cats — planning approval (Animal Keeping)

For more than four breeding cats, an "Animal keeping" application is required under the Planning Scheme:

  • Rural zone, lot at least 20 hectares, fewer than 10 cats — Code assessable
  • All other situations — Impact assessable (public notification required)

See the planning page for what code-assessable and impact-assessable mean in practice. The duty planner can talk through the specifics on 1300 697 372 before you commit to an application.

Note: Microchipping requirements for cats apply regardless of breeder status — every cat you supply must be microchipped before it leaves your care.

faqs.q: What's my legal responsibility for pest animals on my property?
faqs.a:
Every landholder in Queensland has a general biosecurity obligation (GBO) under the Biosecurity Act 2014 — the same law that underpins weed management. In plain terms: if an invasive animal is on your land and there are reasonable, practical steps you could take to limit the damage it does or its spread, you're expected to take them.

General Biosecurity Obligation (GBO): Take all reasonable and practical measures to minimise the biosecurity risk posed by invasive animals under your control. What counts as "reasonable and practical" depends on your situation — a small lifestyle block, a large grazing property, or a suburban home — so there's no one-size-fits-all checklist.

Several species are also formally declared as restricted invasive animals, meaning they must not be moved, kept, fed, given away, sold, or released. For Southern Downs landholders, the ones that come up most often are:

  • Wild dog and dingo (Canis familiaris / Canis familiaris dingo)
  • European red fox (Vulpes vulpes)
  • Feral pig (Sus scrofa)
  • Feral cat (Felis catus) — meaning an unowned cat
  • Rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) — both wild and domestic varieties
  • Feral deer — primarily fallow deer (Dama dama) in the Southern Downs

Indian mynas and some other urban pests are not declared restricted species, but still fall under the GBO and can be managed by landholders — see the Indian myna question below.

For the authoritative species list and control advice, see the Queensland Government — Invasive animals page, or call Council's Local Laws Team on 1300 697 372 for advice specific to your property.

faqs.q: Wild dogs are attacking my stock. What should I do?
faqs.a:
Wild dogs — which includes dingoes, dingo-cross animals, and roaming unowned domestic dogs — are one of the most significant pest animal issues for producers in the Southern Downs. If they're attacking your stock:

  1. Protect remaining stock. Move vulnerable animals — lambing ewes, calving cows, young stock — to paddocks closer to the house or into yards if possible.
  2. Record the evidence. Photograph carcasses, bite patterns, tracks, and scats before you move or dispose of anything. Note GPS locations if you can. This helps officers assess the situation and supports coordinated control.
  3. Report to Council and log the incident in FeralScan. Call 1300 697 372 or use the MySDRC online service request. The free FeralScan app (WildDogScan specifically) lets you log sightings, attacks, and control activity — the data helps Council and neighbours coordinate.
  4. Talk to your neighbours. Wild dogs cover big ranges. Control on one property alone rarely holds for long — the gap fills quickly from surrounding country. A coordinated approach across adjoining properties is the single most effective thing you can do.

Control methods available to landholders include 1080 baiting (the most economical option over large areas — see the baiting question below), trapping with padded foot-hold traps, shooting, and exclusion fencing including cluster fencing arrangements with your neighbours. Livestock guardian animals such as maremma dogs and alpacas are also used successfully by some producers — though they require careful planning if trapping or baiting is also underway nearby.

Council's Local Laws Team can advise on which combination of methods suits your property and help connect you with neighbouring landholders for coordinated programs. Call 1300 697 372.

faqs.q: How does Council's Wild Dog Bounty work?
faqs.a:
Council pays a bounty on wild dogs destroyed within the Southern Downs region as an incentive for ongoing control. Current payment rates:

  • $50 per pup (up to 14 weeks of age)
  • $100 per wild dog (over 14 weeks of age)

How to claim:

  1. Destroy the dog within Southern Downs Regional Council boundaries.
  2. Log the kill in FeralScan — this is required on the claim form.
  3. Present the whole dog (not just a scalp) to a Council Authorised Person within 60 days of destruction.
  4. Complete the Claim for Wild Dog Bounty form. The Authorised Person signs to confirm they received and rendered the dog unsuitable for future claims.
  5. If you haven't claimed a bounty from Council within the last two years, include a completed SDRC Electronic Transfer Form and — if you don't have an ABN — an ABS Statement by Supplier form.
The bounty is designed to complement other control methods — coordinated baiting, exclusion fencing, and guardian animals — rather than replace them. Bounty payments are a privilege, not a legal right, and can be adjusted by Council.

Contact Council's Local Laws Team on 1300 697 372 to confirm current rates and arrange a time to present dogs to an Authorised Person.

faqs.q: Can I hire traps from Council for feral cats or foxes?
faqs.a:
Yes — Council has wire cage traps available for hire to residents dealing with feral cats, stray cats, or foxes on their property. Traps are in regular demand — call ahead to check availability.

How to hire: Complete the Application for Hire of Cat/Fox Trap or Barking Collar or Tree Pear Injector form and submit it — along with proof of identity (driver's licence, passport, or other acceptable ID) — to the Warwick, Stanthorpe, or Allora Customer Service Centre. Hire is for a one-week period.

Fees. Hire is $15 per week or part thereof, with a $100 refundable deposit. The deposit must be claimed within three months of returning the trap, or it will not be refunded. Prices current as of April 2026 and subject to change — see Council's current Fees & Charges schedule for any updates.

Using the trap safely:

  • Check the trap at least twice a day — first thing in the morning and again in the late afternoon.
  • Never leave a baited, set trap unattended for more than 12 hours.
  • Keep the trap out of direct sunlight and provide shade and water if the trap must remain set overnight.
  • Release any non-target animals (possums, native birds, pet cats) immediately and unharmed.

Drop-off: Captured cats can be delivered to Animal Control Officers at the Warwick or Stanthorpe pound, or placed in the 24-hour impoundment drop-off boxes at either facility — these are checked daily, including weekends and public holidays. For foxes, call Council before drop-off for guidance.

Council's Local Laws Team can also advise on trap placement, bait selection, and animal welfare considerations. Call 1300 697 372.

faqs.q: Does Council run a 1080 baiting program? How do I get baits?
faqs.a:
Yes. Council is an authorised supplier of 1080 (sodium fluoroacetate) baits for wild dog and fox control. Two options are available to landholders:

  1. Buy pre-prepared manufactured baits directly from Council — currently $36 for a 10-pack of wild dog baits (April 2026, subject to change). Pickup is available from both the Warwick and Stanthorpe pounds.
  2. Bring your own fresh meat to Council to be injected with 1080 at either the Warwick or Stanthorpe pound. This is often preferred because wild dogs in a particular area may already be habituated to taking a specific meat source from that property.

Before you bait, you must:

  • Attend a baiting briefing or sign the required acknowledgements — Council will guide you through this.
  • Notify all adjoining neighbours at least 72 hours in advance.
  • Erect warning signage at every entrance to your property before baiting begins and leave it in place for at least one month afterwards.
  • Keep working dogs muzzled or restrained, and remove livestock from baited paddocks in accordance with the product label.
1080 is extremely toxic to dogs and there is no reliable antidote. Baits and poisoned carcasses remain toxic for a considerable time — if your working dog or family pet takes a bait or eats a poisoned animal, the outcome is usually fatal. Neighbour notification, signage, and correct bait placement are legal requirements, not guidelines.

Timing: Many landholders bait twice a year — typically March–May (targeting breeding adults) and again September–November (targeting pups and juveniles). Coordinating with your neighbours so baits are out at roughly the same time dramatically improves results.

Call Council's Local Laws Team on 1300 697 372 to arrange bait supply, or to discuss whether baiting is the right approach for your situation.

faqs.q: I've got feral pig damage on my property. What can I do?
faqs.a:
Feral pigs are a restricted invasive animal — they must not be kept, fed, or moved. On rural properties, the common signs are rooting damage to pasture and crops, wallows near water, damaged fences, and lambs or poultry going missing.

Control options that actually work:

  • Trapping with a pig-specific trigger is the most accessible method for small and medium properties. Silo-style cage traps with a funnel entrance or a lift-bar trigger are selective — only pigs will activate them — and pre-feeding for several nights before setting the trigger dramatically improves catch rates.
  • 1080 baiting is the most effective broadscale option but carries the same notification, signage, and pre-feeding requirements as wild dog baiting. Fermented grain is a common and effective bait.
  • Fencing with sheep mesh held tight to the ground, ideally with an electrified offset wire, can protect high-value crops or small paddocks.
  • Ground and aerial shooting can be effective in low-density or open-country situations, and thermal imaging improves detection at night.

Council hires a Hog Hopper. This is a species-specific bait delivery device with a weighted, hinged lid that pigs can lift with their snouts but native animals, macropods, and most livestock cannot. It makes 1080 pig baiting substantially safer by reducing non-target risk, and is particularly useful on properties with wildlife corridors or mixed grazing. Hire is free — a $100 refundable deposit applies, maximum hire period two weeks, deposit claimable within three months of return. Call 1300 697 372 to arrange.

Pigs have large home ranges and breed rapidly — a control program on one property alone is rarely enough. Coordinate with your neighbours whenever you can.

Feral pigs can carry diseases transmissible to humans — leptospirosis, brucellosis, Q fever, melioidosis, and others. Wear gloves and avoid direct contact with blood, urine, or faeces. Don't eat undercooked feral pig meat, and don't feed raw feral pig meat or offal to dogs (swine brucellosis can pass from pigs to dogs to humans).

Council's Local Laws Team can discuss trap designs, arrange bait supply, and help coordinate control across adjoining properties. Call 1300 697 372.

faqs.q: I've got a rabbit problem. What should I do?
faqs.a:
Queensland is the only Australian state that maintains a designated rabbit-free zone, protected by a rabbit-proof fence and actively managed by the Darling Downs-Moreton Rabbit Board (DDMRB). The Southern Downs sits inside this zone — which is why rabbit sightings here are treated seriously.

If you see a wild rabbit in the Southern Downs, report it promptly to the DDMRB on 07 4661 4076 or to Council on 1300 697 372. The DDMRB has specialist officers for rabbit control within the protected zone.

Pet rabbits are illegal in Queensland. Domestic and wild rabbits are the same species and will interbreed if domestic rabbits escape. Keeping a pet rabbit — even a desexed one in a secure hutch — is not permitted. Permits are only issued for research or certain forms of public entertainment (e.g. magic shows, circuses).

If you currently have a pet rabbit, do not release it into the wild. Options:

  • Surrender it to Council at the Warwick or Stanthorpe office.
  • Contact the Darling Downs-Moreton Rabbit Board on 07 4661 4076 to arrange collection.
  • Arrange for humane euthanasia through a veterinarian.

Council and the DDMRB would rather help you resolve a pet rabbit situation than see one released — so get in touch, and no one will be unpleasant about it.

faqs.q: Are feral deer a problem in the Southern Downs?
faqs.a:
Yes — and the Southern Downs has the distinction of being home to the largest wild fallow deer herd in Queensland, centred on the Pikedale area south-west of Warwick. Fallow deer were first released on the Darling Downs around Westbrook and Warwick between 1870 and 1872, and the Pikedale herd is now broadly continuous with the large New England Tableland population across the NSW border. For most landholders in the region, deer are a quiet background fact of rural life more than a front-of-mind problem — but if they're damaging crops, pasture, or fences on your property, the following applies.

Species. Fallow deer (Dama dama) is the species to know locally. Queensland also has established populations of red, chital, and rusa deer, but those herds are well north and east of the Southern Downs.

Legal status. Feral fallow deer are a category 3, 4 and 6 restricted invasive animal under the Biosecurity Act 2014. They must not be moved, fed, given away, sold, or released. The same general biosecurity obligation (GBO) that applies to other invasive animals applies here — take reasonable and practical steps to minimise the biosecurity risk on land you control.

Farmed deer and deer in game parks are treated separately and must be kept in deer-proof enclosures. If an enclosed deer escapes and establishes in the wild, the owner is responsible under the Act. Anyone keeping deer needs to register as a biosecurity entity.

Control options for landholders:

  • Ground shooting is considered the most effective and humane method currently available — usually done at night from a vehicle with spotlights or thermal equipment, by trained personnel with appropriate firearms licences.
  • Helicopter shooting can be cost-effective across large or open properties but is a specialised operation that's best coordinated across multiple adjoining landholders.
  • Trapping is sometimes an option in peri-urban areas where shooting isn't practical — typically a trip-wire activated self-closing gate or clover trap. Traps must be checked frequently and animals promptly tranquilised or euthanased; animal welfare considerations are significant.
  • Exclusion fencing works but is expensive. A proper deer fence is around 2.1m high with heavy-duty strainers, 9m post spacing, and netting pegged to the ground. Usually only practical for protecting high-value crops or farmed enclosures rather than whole properties.
  • Engaging licensed recreational hunters is a common approach among local landholders. Think through access conditions, public liability insurance, and references before allowing anyone on your property.

Coordination matters. Deer have large home ranges and move between properties freely. Control on a single property is usually eroded by in-migration from surrounding country — so coordinated effort across several adjoining landholders is much more effective than anyone working alone. Council's Local Laws Team and local Landcare groups can help connect landholders working on the same issue.

For species identification, detailed control guidance, and the Queensland Feral Deer Management Strategy 2022–27, see Biosecurity Queensland — Invasive animals. To discuss deer on your property or in your area, call Council's Local Laws Team on 1300 697 372.

faqs.q: My neighbour's cat keeps coming onto my property. What are my options?
faqs.a:
Roaming cats are a common nuisance complaint. The best first step is almost always a friendly conversation with the cat's owner — in many cases they don't realise the cat is causing a problem, and a calm chat resolves it without Council involvement.

If a direct conversation isn't possible or doesn't help:

  1. Hire a cat trap from Council — see the trap hire question above. They're routinely used for exactly this situation — call ahead to check availability.
  2. Drop the captured cat at the Warwick or Stanthorpe pound. 24-hour impoundment boxes are available and checked daily, including weekends and public holidays.
  3. If the cat is microchipped, Council will attempt to contact the owner. Cats with a microchip identifying an owner are held for a minimum of five days; cats with no form of ID are held for a minimum of three days before being assessed for rehoming (often via Southern Downs Ark) or other disposition.
Council runs a subsidised cat desexing and microchipping program through the National Desexing Network, subject to available funding each year. Desexed cats are less likely to roam or fight, and a current microchip is the single best way to make sure a lost cat comes home. Call 1300 697 372 to check current eligibility and availability.

faqs.q: Indian mynas are nesting in my roof or making a mess. What can I do?
faqs.a:
Indian mynas are not a declared restricted species, but they're still covered by the general biosecurity obligation — and Council supports residents who want to control them. They compete aggressively for tree hollows, evict native parrots, and roof nests can introduce mites, lice, and a fire risk.

Don't confuse Indian mynas with native noisy miners. They look superficially similar but noisy miners are native and protected. Quick ID: Indian mynas have a brown body and bright yellow legs; noisy miners are grey with flesh-coloured legs. Both have yellow bills and yellow eye patches. Destroying a noisy miner is a wildlife offence.

What actually reduces Indian myna numbers:

  • Block access to nest sites in your roof and eaves. Cover gaps, clear dead palm fronds promptly, and bird-proof gutters. Check for trapped possums before sealing permanently.
  • Don't feed them, even accidentally. Bring pet food inside, feed livestock where mynas can't reach it, and seal compost and food scraps. Bird feeders set out for native species often become myna feeders instead.
  • Remove nests and eggs (wearing gloves). Indian myna eggs are a distinctive blue-turquoise colour — no native hollow-nesting bird lays eggs that colour, so if you see them in your roof, you've got mynas. Seal eggs and nest material in a plastic bag and put it in your wheelie bin.
  • Restore native habitat. Mynas prefer cleared, disturbed land; planting local natives and reducing lawn area makes your property less attractive to them and more welcoming for native species.

Trapping is also possible but requires careful planning, access to humane euthanasia, and enough coordination with neighbours to actually make a dent in the local population. If you're interested in setting up or joining a community action group, the Indian Myna Action Group publishes detailed guidance. Council can advise on local considerations.

faqs.q: There are pest animals on Council land or roads near my property. Who do I contact?
faqs.a:
Council's Local Laws Team coordinates invasive animal control on Council-managed land and road reserves. Report via Council's online service request form or call 1300 697 372. Helpful details to include: location (GPS or nearest cross-street), species, approximate number of animals, time of sighting, and any evidence of damage.

Not all public land is Council-managed. State-controlled roads — including the New England Highway and Cunningham Highway — are managed by the Department of Transport and Main Roads; call TMR on 13 20 80. National parks (Main Range, Girraween, Sundown) are managed by Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service — contact QPWS for pest issues inside the park boundary.

For region-wide sighting data, consider logging reports in FeralScan as well. It's free, works as a phone app, and the accumulated data helps Council, DDMRB, and neighbouring landholders coordinate broader control efforts.

faqs.q: Do I have to control weeds on my property?
faqs.a:
Generally, yes — but the obligation is more practical than most people expect. Queensland law asks every landholder to take "reasonable and practical" steps to prevent the spread of invasive plants from their land. That's the standard, rather than a requirement to eradicate every weed.

What "reasonable and practical" looks like depends on the species, the size of the infestation, the size of the property, and what the landholder can realistically manage. Treating a small new outbreak of African Boxthorn is reasonable; hand-pulling every blackberry on 200 hectares of bushland is not.

A few species do come with stronger obligations:

  • Blackberry, African Boxthorn, and Lantana are restricted invasive plants under the state Biosecurity Act 2014 — they must not be sold, given away, or released into the environment, and active control is expected.
  • Firethorn, Green Cestrum, and St John's Wort are declared pest plants under Council's local law, which gives Council the authority to take further action if needed.

Council's Local Laws Team can help you work out what's reasonable for your property — call 1300 697 372.

faqs.q: Which weeds are a problem in the Southern Downs?
faqs.a:
A handful of species cause most of the grief locally. Each has a Queensland Government fact sheet with identification photos, life-cycle information, and detailed herbicide recommendations.

Restricted invasive plants under the Biosecurity Act 2014 (statewide — cannot be sold, given away, or released):

  • African Boxthorn — spiny shrub, forms impenetrable thickets, harbours rabbits and foxes. A Weed of National Significance.
  • Blackberry — dense thickets, invades pastures and bushland, found around Stanthorpe, Warwick, and Killarney. A Weed of National Significance.
  • Lantana — common on recently purchased or neglected land, smothers native vegetation, toxic to stock.

Locally declared under Council's Subordinate Local Law No. 7 (Council can issue control notices):

  • Firethorn — spiny ornamental that has escaped gardens; common on the Granite Belt between Warwick and the border.
  • Green Cestrum — toxic to cattle, sheep, horses, pigs, and poultry; spreads from roots and by birds.
  • St John's Wort — causes photosensitivity in grazing stock; known populations around Stanthorpe.

Other priority species:

  • Tree Pear and other invasive cacti — Council offers free Cactus Injectors for landholders to treat on their own property (see equipment hire question below).

For the full state list of invasive plants with individual fact sheets: Queensland Government — Invasive plants fact sheets. For the SDRC Pest Management page: Pest Management — Weeds.

faqs.q: I've found a plant I think might be a weed. How do I identify it?
faqs.a:
The Queensland Government publishes free fact sheets for every declared and restricted invasive plant — complete with identification photos, distinguishing features, and look-alike species. Start there: Queensland Government — Invasive plants fact sheets.

If you're still not sure, Council's Local Laws Team can help. Call 1300 697 372 and describe what you've seen — leaf shape, flower colour, fruit, where it's growing, how tall it is. Local Laws may request a photo to assist with identification.

Be careful with general image-search tools for plant ID — many invasive plants have native look-alikes, and getting it wrong in either direction is a problem (destroying a native, or ignoring a declared weed). The Queensland fact sheets are the definitive source.

faqs.q: What herbicide should I use?
faqs.a:
Every Queensland Government weed fact sheet includes a detailed herbicide table — with specific products, application rates, situations (pasture, non-crop, native conservation area), and the right season to spray. These are the authoritative source and worth printing before you head to the rural supplies store.

Queensland Government — Invasive plants fact sheets.

A few general principles:

  • Always read the herbicide label and apply strictly in accordance with it. Labels are legally binding.
  • Check for permits. Some herbicide uses rely on APVMA minor-use permits — where one applies, the current permit number is noted in the species fact sheet.
  • Timing matters. Most weeds are best treated when actively growing — typically spring through autumn. Spraying dormant or stressed plants wastes chemical and gives poor results.
  • Remove grazing stock from sprayed areas during and after treatment — treated plants can become more palatable or temporarily more toxic.
  • Some properties are in hazardous chemical areas under the Agricultural Chemicals Distribution Control Act 1966, which restricts certain herbicides. Check before applying.

Council's Local Laws Team can offer general advice on approach, but cannot recommend specific commercial products. Call 1300 697 372 to discuss.

faqs.q: There are weeds on a Council road near my property. Who do I contact?
faqs.a:
Council's Local Laws Team coordinates weed control on Council roads and land. Report via Council's online service request form or call 1300 697 372.

Weeds on the New England Highway or Cunningham Highway? These are State Government roads managed by TMR — contact TMR on 13 20 80.

faqs.q: My neighbour has weeds spreading onto my property. Can Council help?
faqs.a:
Yes — this is a biosecurity matter rather than a "neighbour dispute." Every landholder in Queensland has a legal duty to take reasonable steps to prevent the spread of invasive plants from their land. If that duty isn't being met and weeds are crossing onto your property, Council can investigate.

Practical first step: speak to your neighbour if it feels safe to do so. In many cases the issue is that the landholder doesn't know what's on their property or doesn't realise the plant is a problem. A friendly conversation often achieves more than a formal complaint.

If that doesn't resolve the issue, lodge a service request via Council's online service request form or call 1300 697 372 and ask to speak to a Local Laws Officer. Council's Local Laws Team will assess the situation and discuss next steps with you — which may include working with the neighbouring landholder directly, or — for restricted species covered by the state Biosecurity Act 2014 — referring the matter to Biosecurity Queensland (part of the Department of Primary Industries). See the DPI contact page.

faqs.q: I've been told I have a water leak. How do I find it?
faqs.a:
Many leaks can be found without a plumber. Check inside first — a running toilet is a common cause. Also check all taps, showerheads, and washing machine connections.

Outside, look for unusually green or boggy ground — this can indicate an underground pipe failure even when there's no visible surface water. Check garden timers and hose guns too.

The Checking for Water Leaks Fact Sheet details methods for detecting water leaks, including in underground pipes without a plumber.

faqs.q: There's a leak at the meter or on the footpath — is that Council's responsibility?
faqs.a:
Council's side (the meter itself, or the pipe between the water main and the meter): report to Council immediately on 1300 697 372.

Your side (the pipe running from the meter into the property): this is the property owner's responsibility. Consider shutting off the water at the meter while you arrange a licensed plumber.

Not sure which side? Call 1300 697 372 and we can help work it out.

faqs.q: Can I get a rates adjustment if I had an unexpected leak?
faqs.a: In rare circumstances Council may consider an adjustment for water lost to an undetected leak. Contact Council's Revenue Team on 1300 697 372 to discuss. Having your repair invoice available will assist with the assessment.

faqs.q: How can I monitor my water usage between bills?
faqs.a: The My SDRC Water portal connects to your Smart Water Meter and lets you view near-real-time usage and set a custom alert threshold to catch a leak early. Sign-up details are on page 4 of your rates notice. See also: Smart Water Meters.

faqs.q: Where is my water meter?
faqs.a: Water meters are usually near the front boundary of the property close to the street — often in a small covered box set into the ground. If you can't find yours, call 1300 697 372 and we can look up the exact location for your address.

faqs.q: Where do I take this? — Recycle Mate does the thinking for you
faqs.a:
Recycle Mate is a free app (and web tool) that tells you exactly how and where to dispose of almost anything. Snap a photo or type the item name, and it returns locations specific to the Southern Downs — including Council waste facilities, supermarkets running soft plastic or battery collection, pharmacies taking unused medication, and charity shops accepting reusable items.

It's the fastest way to answer "where does this go?" without having to call Council. Download from the app store, or use the SDRC Recycle Mate page.

If Recycle Mate doesn't cover your item, or you'd like to double-check, call Council on 1300 697 372 and the waste team can advise.

faqs.q: What day is my bin collected?
faqs.a: Your collection day is tied to your property address. Search your address using SDRC's online mapping tool to find your bin day, or call 1300 697 372. Collection days may change on public holidays — Council will publish any changes in advance.

faqs.q: What goes in which bin?
faqs.a:
Red or Green lid (general waste, weekly) — kitchen and food waste, general household rubbish, plastic bags and cling wrap, nappies, and polystyrene foam.

Yellow lid (recycling, fortnightly) — paper and cardboard, steel and aluminium cans, rigid plastic bottles and containers (lids removed), glass bottles and jars (lids removed).

Not sure about a specific item? Use Recycle Mate (first question above) — it's built exactly for this.

Never put batteries in either bin — they can cause serious truck fires. See the batteries question below.

Full detail: What goes in my bins — SDRC.

faqs.q: My bin wasn't collected. What do I do?
faqs.a:
Lodge a request via Council's online service request form or call 1300 697 372. Cleanaway will schedule a return collection before your next regular collection day.

Before you lodge: confirm the bin was at the kerbside by 6:00am and wasn't blocked by a parked vehicle — these are the most common reasons a bin is passed.

faqs.q: My bin is damaged or missing. Can I get a replacement?
faqs.a: Yes. Lodge a request via Council's online service request form or call 1300 697 372. Include your address and describe the issue. Damaged bins are repaired where possible; if a bin is not serviceable or has been stolen, it will be replaced.

faqs.q: I'm elderly or have a disability and can't put my bins out. Is there help available?
faqs.a:
Yes. Council offers an Infirm Collection Service for residents unable to put bins out due to age, disability, or medical immobility. Cleanaway drivers collect the bins from the property and return them once emptied, as part of their normal round.

The service is only available if nobody else at the property is able to present the bins. To apply, email mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au with a letter requesting the service and a confirmation letter or medical certificate from a registered health practitioner (subject line: ATTN Waste Team).

faqs.q: I don't have a bin service — can I get one?
faqs.a:
Depends where the property sits in the Designated Waste Collection Area. There are three categories:

  • Compulsory — service is mandatory and the charge appears on your rates notice.
  • Opt-In / Opt-Out — you may choose whether to take the service.
  • Voluntary — you can request a service, and Cleanaway decides whether the property can be serviced based on route and access.

To request a new service, email mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au with a letter requesting the service and accepting that charges will be added to your rates notice (subject line: ATTN Waste Team). If approved, bins are delivered to the property.

Properties outside the collection area entirely can access one of Council's waste facilities directly, or use a rural bin compound if one services your area. These are locked, unsupervised bin compounds — access is by key, issued only to approved residents within the catchment area. Call 1300 697 372 to check whether your property falls within a compound catchment.
