faqs.q: How do I dispose of green waste, garden clippings, and trickle tape?
faqs.a:
Green waste — grass clippings, prunings, small branches, and similar — can go in your red or green lid general waste bin. Do not put green waste in the yellow recycling bin.

Larger loads can be taken to a Council waste facility. Green waste disposal is free for residents; commercial green waste attracts a disposal fee. Recycling at home through composting or mulching is also a great option — see Council's Worm Farming and Composting fact sheets.

Trickle tape (T-tape) — Council stockpiles clean trickle tape for recycling at the Stanthorpe Waste Management Facility, free of charge. The tape must be separated from plastic mulch and as free as possible from soil, roots, and organic matter. Tape that's contaminated cannot be recycled and attracts landfill fees for commercial operators. Site supervisors will direct you to the stockpile on arrival.

Please don't dump green waste on bushland, verges, or waterways — it spreads pest plants, fuels bushfires, and can attract wildlife to roadsides. See "Reporting illegal dumping" below.

faqs.q: How do I dispose of batteries, phones, and e-waste?
faqs.a:
Never put batteries in a kerbside bin. They can short-circuit, catch fire, and damage trucks or facilities. This is one of the fastest-growing causes of waste fires in Australia.

Batteries under 5kg — Council has partnered with Ecobatt, and dedicated battery collection containers are available at all supervised Council waste facilities. Best practice is to tape the terminals (particularly on lithium batteries) and hand the battery to a facility attendant rather than dropping it in. Accepted types include:

  • Household alkaline — AA, AAA, C, D, PP3, button cells
  • Lithium / rechargeable — mobile phones, laptops, tablets, cameras, e-cigarettes and vapes, portable tools, e-scooters and bikes, power banks
  • Lead acid — car, vehicle, caravan batteries (ensure caps are tight; speak to an attendant if the casing is damaged)

Recycle Mate also lists private drop-off points — many pharmacies, supermarkets, and electronics retailers run their own battery and phone collection programs, which may be closer than a waste facility.

E-waste (computers, TVs, accessories) is accepted at all supervised Council waste facilities for recycling. Damaged batteries — speak to a facility attendant before attending.

faqs.q: Where do I take items I can't put in the bin — mattresses, whitegoods, chemicals, asbestos?
faqs.a:
Start with Recycle Mate — it will often find a closer or cheaper option than a Council facility. For most other items, Council's waste facilities accept them directly. Locations, opening hours, and accepted materials are on the Waste Facilities page.

Free at Council facilities: scrap metal, clean concrete and bricks, e-waste, empty agvet chemical containers (drumMUSTER), used motor oil at some sites, and clean timber pallets.

Fees apply to: general household waste, mattresses, tyres, whitegoods, construction and demolition waste. Fees are set in Council's annual Fees & Charges schedule.

Asbestos — pre-booking required. Asbestos must be double-bagged in 200-micron plastic, clearly labelled, and pre-booked with Council before attending the facility. Facility staff cannot accept asbestos without a booking. Call 1300 697 372 to arrange.

Deceased pets — small pets (birds, fish, guinea pigs) can go in the general waste bin. Larger pets should be taken to the closest accepting waste facility; burial is only available at the Warwick Waste Management Facility. Prior notice is required for bulk loads.

Ammunition, explosives, and old fireworks — never go in any bin or waste facility. Contact the Queensland Explosives Inspectorate on 1300 739 868 (24-hour hotline).

faqs.q: Someone has dumped rubbish on my land or in a public place. How do I report it?
faqs.a:
Illegal dumping is any unlawful deposit of 200 litres or more of waste — roughly the volume of a wheelie bin — in bushland, roadsides, waterways, outside charity bins, on the kerbside outside of collection time, or at the wrong location within a waste facility.

Lodge a service request via Council's online service request form or by calling 1300 697 372. You can pin the exact location on the map and attach photos directly through the form.

Include as much detail as you can:

  • Time, date, place, and description of the waste
  • Vehicle registration, make, model, colour, or distinguishing features
  • Description of the person (location in vehicle, clothing, gender)
Don't approach the person depositing the waste. Take photos only if safe to do so.

Fines are significant — individuals and corporations can face substantial on-the-spot penalties, with much higher amounts available if the matter goes to court. Current figures are in the Illegal Dumping fact sheet.

Worth knowing: almost all domestic waste can be disposed of at Council facilities for free. The cost of doing it properly is much less than the fine for dumping.

faqs.q: I've spotted what looks like trade waste pollution — chemicals in a waterway, oil drums leaking, or unauthorised dumping of business waste. How do I report it?
faqs.a:
Trade waste and environmental pollution is a more serious matter than ordinary illegal dumping, and Council takes it seriously. Examples include dumped solvents or chemicals, oil drums or tanks leaking onto land or into waterways, contaminated runoff from a workshop or industrial site, sediment escaping a construction site, and unauthorised landfilling on private land.

How to report:

  • Lodge a service request via Council's online service request form — no account required, and you can attach photos and pin the location on a map.
  • Or call 1300 697 372.
  • For incidents in progress that may pose an immediate risk to people, animals, or waterways, call 000 for police or fire emergency response, then notify Council afterwards.

Helpful details to include:

  • Time, date, and exact location (a dropped pin or street address)
  • Description of what you saw — substance, container type, smell, colour, volume
  • Vehicle details if relevant — make, model, colour, registration
  • Photos, if you can take them safely

Council's regulatory services team investigates illegal dumping of trade waste and works alongside Queensland State Government authorities where the matter falls under state environmental laws. Larger-scale or hazardous incidents are typically escalated for joint investigation. Reporting these matters protects waterways, soil, and your community — please don't assume someone else has called it in.

Don't approach the source. Take photos only if it's safe. Some dumped substances are genuinely dangerous, and the priority is your safety and an accurate report rather than confronting whoever's responsible.

faqs.q: There's an abandoned shopping trolley near my property. Whose problem is it?
faqs.a:
Almost always the retailer's, not Council's. Most major supermarkets and hardware chains in the Southern Downs (Coles, Woolworths, Aldi, IGA, Bunnings) contract trolley-collection services that respond same-day or next-day to reported abandoned trolleys.

What to do:

  • Look for a sticker on the trolley with a phone number or QR code — this is the fastest path. The trolley-collection contractor will arrange retrieval directly.
  • If the trolley has no sticker or you can't identify the retailer, call the nearest store of the chain it belongs to — they'll arrange collection.
  • If a trolley remains uncollected for an extended period, or is repeatedly dumped at a particular location, lodge a service request with Council. Council can follow up with the retailer under local nuisance provisions, but it's a slower path than going direct.

Trolleys left in waterways, storm drains, or causing immediate hazards (blocking footpaths, on roads) can be reported to Council on 1300 697 372 for prompt action.

faqs.q: How do I report a pothole or road damage?
faqs.a: Report online using Council's online service request form — the request form has a map for marking the exact location of the pothole. Alternatively call 1300 697 372. Include the street name, nearest landmark, and an estimate of the size.

faqs.q: Are damaged roads Council's or the State Government's responsibility?
faqs.a:
Not all roads in the region are Council's responsibility. Major highways are managed by the Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR).

  • State roads (New England Hwy, Cunningham Hwy, other TMR roads): contact TMR — 13 20 80
  • Rail crossings / railway tracks: contact Queensland Rail — 13 16 17
  • Council roads: lodge a request with Council as above

Not sure? Call Council on 1300 697 372 and we can help.

faqs.q: How do I check if a road is closed?
faqs.a: The SDRC Disaster Dashboard has current road closure information and a map tool that has flood camera images of key crossings — the most up-to-date source during weather events. For State roads check Queensland Traffic.

faqs.q: My vehicle was damaged by a road defect. Can I make a claim?
faqs.a: You can submit a letter of demand to Council. Include your name, time and location of the incident, nature of the damage, and any supporting evidence. For road-related claims address to: ATTN: Governance, Southern Downs Regional Council, PO Box 26, Warwick QLD 4370, or email mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au.

faqs.q: What disputes can Council help with?
faqs.a:
Council's Local Laws team can investigate: persistent noise nuisances (barking dogs, loud machinery, amplified music); dust, smoke, odour, or light pollution; water pollution from a neighbouring property; unauthorised building works or illegal use of a structure; and unlawful land use.

Lodge a complaint via Council's online service request form or call 1300 697 372.

faqs.q: What disputes are outside Council's jurisdiction?
faqs.a: Some common disputes are private matters Council cannot mediate or enforce — including boundary and fencing disputes, trees crossing property lines, parking complaints outside the regulated Warwick CBD parking area (a police matter), and easement disputes. For these matters the Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal (QCAT) is often the right avenue: qcat.qld.gov.au or 1300 753 228.

faqs.q: My neighbour's tree drops branches, blocks light, or damages my fence. What can I do?
faqs.a:
Tree disputes between neighbours are a private matter that Council cannot mediate. They fall under the Queensland Neighbourhood Disputes (Dividing Fences and Trees) Act 2011.

Practical steps:

  1. Talk to your neighbour first. Most tree issues are resolved when the owner is made aware.
  2. If you can't reach an agreement, you may serve a formal notice on the tree owner under the Act requesting action.
  3. If that doesn't work, the matter can be taken to QCAT: qcat.qld.gov.au or 1300 753 228.

You have a right to trim branches that overhang your property up to the boundary line, at your own cost, provided you don't damage the tree's health. Return the trimmings to the tree owner (don't dump them).

Trees on Council land or road reserves are a different matter — lodge a service request and a Council officer will assess. Never trim or remove a Council tree yourself.

faqs.q: I have a boundary or fencing dispute with my neighbour. What now?
faqs.a:
Fencing between two residential properties is governed by the Neighbourhood Disputes (Dividing Fences and Trees) Act 2011 — not Council. The general rule is that both neighbours share the cost of a "sufficient dividing fence" equally, but what counts as sufficient depends on the zone and existing fence.

Practical steps:

  1. Talk to your neighbour first. Agree on what needs doing and get a quote from a fencing contractor.
  2. If you can't agree, serve a formal Notice to Fence on your neighbour. Templates are available from the Queensland Government.
  3. If there's still no agreement 30 days after the notice, either party can apply to QCAT for a decision: qcat.qld.gov.au or 1300 753 228.

Boundary disputes (where the fence should sit) are separate from fencing disputes (who pays for what). If you're uncertain where the boundary actually is, a licensed surveyor can confirm. Council's online mapping shows cadastral boundaries for reference, but is not a substitute for a survey.

faqs.q: My neighbour's shed or extension looks unapproved. How do I report it?
faqs.a:
Unapproved building works are something Council can investigate — unlike most neighbour disputes. If you believe a structure has been built without the required building or planning approval, lodge a complaint via Council's online service request form or call 1300 697 372.

Include as much detail as you can: the address, a description of the structure, when it was built (if known), and why you believe it's unapproved.

Council's Building Compliance team will investigate and, if the works are unapproved, may issue a notice requiring retrospective certification or removal. The process takes time — compliance is not usually a same-day outcome.

Not every structure requires approval. Small sheds (under 10m²), fences under 2m, and retaining walls under 1m may be self-assessable. See the Building Rural or Building Urban FAQ for the specifics.

faqs.q: Someone is running a business from a residential property. Can Council investigate?
faqs.a:
Yes — "unlawful land use" is a matter Council can investigate under the Planning Scheme. Some home-based businesses are permitted (typically small-scale, low-impact operations that don't generate traffic, noise, or signage beyond residential norms). Others require planning approval or simply aren't permitted in residential zones.

Common triggers that cross the line: commercial vehicle traffic, employees arriving and leaving, customer parking, commercial signage, industrial noise, or activities that change the character of the property.

Lodge a complaint via Council's online service request form or call 1300 697 372. Council's Planning Compliance team will investigate.

faqs.q: My rate notice shows a new “NPPR” category. What is it?
faqs.a:
NPPR is Council's new Non-Principal Place of Residence general rate category, introduced in the 2026/27 budget for residential properties that aren't the owner's main home (rentals, holiday houses, second homes).

It has its own tab covering how the rate is calculated, the test for whether your property should be NPPR, and how to object if you've been miscategorised: see NPPR Rates.

faqs.q: How do I pay my rates?
faqs.a: Rates can be paid online via SDRC Online Payments, by BPAY (biller code and reference on your notice), or in person at the Warwick or Stanthorpe office. You can also pay by post — cheque payable to Southern Downs Regional Council, PO Box 26, Warwick QLD 4370.

faqs.q: I'm struggling to pay my rates. What can I do?
faqs.a: Contact Council as early as possible on 1300 697 372. Options may include instalment arrangements, hardship provisions, or deferral in exceptional circumstances — the sooner you contact us, the more options are available. See the Payment Difficulties page for more information.

faqs.q: How do I receive my rates notice by email instead of post?
faqs.a: Scan the QR code on page 2 of your rates notice to register for eNotices and receive future notices by email — faster, paperless, and you're notified as soon as your notice is ready.

faqs.q: How do I check my rates balance?
faqs.a:
Two ways:

  • Call Council on 1300 697 372 and quote your property address or rates account number — Customer Service can give you a current balance over the phone.
  • Sign up for eProperty — a free online portal that lets you view your current rates balance, payment history, and rates notices any time. Visit Council's eProperty registration page to set up an account. You'll need a recent rates notice handy to verify your details.

faqs.q: When do my rates notices arrive in the post?
faqs.a:
Council issues two rates notices per year:

  • First notice — arrives in February or March, covering the first half of the financial year.
  • Second notice — arrives in August or September, covering the second half.

If it's been more than three weeks past the expected delivery and your notice hasn't arrived, call Council on 1300 697 372 to confirm your postal address and request a replacement copy. Or sign up for eProperty (see above) to receive notices electronically — faster, free, and avoids postal delays.

faqs.q: I've received a supplementary rates notice. What does it mean?
faqs.a:
A supplementary rates notice is an additional charge issued between the regular six-monthly notices, usually because something has changed about how your property is rated. The most common trigger is a property sale or subdivision involving bulk-assessed land.

What is bulk assessment? In rural zones, it's common for several adjoining lots under the same ownership to be rated as a single Property ID (PID). The State Government values them collectively — usually at a lower per-hectare rate than they'd be valued individually. When one of those lots is sold or subdivided, it gets its own PID and is revalued independently. The new individual valuation is typically higher than its previous proportional share, which means the rates change.

Why is the bill higher than I expected?

  • A standard rates notice covers a six-month period. A supplementary notice may cover a longer period — sometimes a full year or more — depending on when the change took effect. Always check the dates the notice covers before comparing it to a regular notice.
  • If the change was a subdivision or split from bulk-assessed land, the higher valuation reflects the State Government's per-lot revaluation. Council has no discretion to reduce a State-set valuation.

What can I do if I disagree with the valuation? Property valuations are set by the Queensland Department of Resources, not Council. Owners have 60 days from the date of the valuation notice to lodge a formal objection with the Department. Council cannot intervene in this process — but Customer Service can help you understand what's on your supplementary notice. Call 1300 697 372 if you want to talk through the charge.

Property sale settlements: During a typical settlement, solicitors adjust the sale price so that rates owing for the current period are shared between vendor and purchaser in proportion to their respective periods of ownership. Neither party usually needs to contact Council — the change of name on the property is handled automatically by the Titles Office. For bulk-assessed properties being split or sold, however, the standard practice is for the vendor to ensure all rates are paid in full before settlement, since revaluation typically can't happen quickly enough to issue a supplementary notice during the settlement period.

faqs.q: What do the different charges on my rates notice mean?
faqs.a: The Rates & Charges Explained page breaks down each line item — what it funds and how it's calculated. For a specific question about your notice, call 1300 697 372 and a rates officer can walk through it with you.

faqs.q: What is the NPPR category, and why was it introduced?
faqs.a:
NPPR stands for Non-Principal Place of Residence. It's a general rate category, introduced in the 2026/27 budget, for residential properties that aren't the owner's main home. A person can have only one principal place of residence — all of their other residential properties fall into NPPR.

Council's stated reason for the change is to keep general rates lower for owner-occupiers: rather than spreading a larger increase across everyone, the 2026/27 budget held the median owner-occupier increase below CPI — lower than many Queensland councils — with residential and business rates kept lower as a result. Before adopting the budget, Council ran extensive community engagement, with the proposed NPPR category outlined as part of that process.

The NPPR category affects only the general rate part of your notice. Charges for water access and usage, sewerage, waste collection and the emergency services levy are calculated independently — current amounts for those are in Council's Revenue Statement.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council's NPPR information (updated August 2026), the 6 August 2026 media release, and the objection form (v5, 27 July 2026)

faqs.q: How is the NPPR general rate calculated, and how much more is it?
faqs.a:
Like all general rates, the NPPR levy is calculated from your land valuation. There are two NPPR sub-categories, split at a land value of $239,000:

CategoryLand valueNPPR rate (per $1 of land value)Owner-occupier rate
NPPR 1Less than $239,0001.103c0.919c
NPPR 2Greater than $239,0000.882c0.735c

Both work out to a 20% higher rate in the dollar than the comparable owner-occupier category. NPPR 1 properties also have a minimum general rate charge of $1,700.00 per year.

Two other things affect the final figure: your land value may have changed since your last notice — you should have been notified by the Valuer-General if so, or you can check your current land valuation online — and there is currently a 35% cap on the year-on-year increase in your rates charge.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council's NPPR information (updated August 2026), the 6 August 2026 media release, and the objection form (v5, 27 July 2026)

faqs.q: Is my property a principal place of residence or NPPR? The three-part test
faqs.a:
Your property is your principal place of residence (PPR) if all three of these are true:

  • 1. A natural person owns it (or holds a life tenancy) — not a company, trust, person as trustee, incorporated association, personal representative or deceased estate.
  • 2. You live there — at least 245 days per year (about 8 months) — and intend to keep doing so.
  • 3. It's a lawful dwelling (Class 1a) — evidenced by a Form 21 Final Inspection Certificate, or a current Permission to Occupy Temporary Accommodation under Council's Subordinate Local Law 1.3 (the objection form calls this a Temporary Home Permit).

Fail any one of the three and the property is NPPR. Remember: only one PPR per person — every other residential property you own is NPPR even if family members live there.

Life tenant — a person who holds a legal right to use, occupy or benefit from a property for the duration of their natural life (for example, under a will).
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council's NPPR information (updated August 2026), the 6 August 2026 media release, and the objection form (v5, 27 July 2026)

faqs.q: How do common situations get categorised? (trusts, aged care, Airbnb, vacant land, deceased estates)
faqs.a:
Some frequent scenarios:

  • Company or trust owns it, and I live there: a property 100% owned by a company or trust is NPPR — the ownership test requires a natural person, with no exceptions — including where an occupant holds a life tenancy.
  • Owner in aged care: the home stays PPR if the owner lived there before entering care, intends to return, and the home stays unoccupied (not rented out).
  • Short-term accommodation (e.g. Airbnb): licensed short-term accommodation is rated in a Commercial category rather than NPPR (a licence is required). If the owner also lives on site, it may still qualify as PPR — contact Council's revenue team on 1300 697 372 to discuss.
  • Vacant land, or a home under construction: NPPR until a Form 21 is issued and you're living there. Exception: a current Permission to Occupy Temporary Accommodation makes it PPR — see the Building Rural tab for living on site during a build.
  • Mail goes to a PO box: that alone doesn't make a property NPPR — run the three-part test, and object if the categorisation is wrong.
  • Deceased estate: NPPR — unless a life tenant under the will lives in the property, which is a PPR pathway.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council's NPPR information (updated August 2026), the 6 August 2026 media release, and the objection form (v5, 27 July 2026)

faqs.q: I believe my property has been wrongly categorised. How do I object?
faqs.a:
Under the Local Government Regulation 2012, you can lodge a Notice of Objection Against Categorisation. The only ground for objection is that the category is factually wrong — i.e. the property really is your main home (or otherwise belongs in a different category). Disagreement with the policy itself isn't a ground of objection (see below for how to give that feedback).

Two ways to lodge:

  • Online: lodge an online service request and choose “Notice of Objection Against Categorisation”. Have your rate notice handy — you'll need your Property ID, address, current rating category and land use code, all shown on the notice.
  • Paper form: download the Notice of Objection Against Categorisation form from the Rates and Property Forms section of Council's website, and email the completed form with your evidence to mail@sdrc.qld.gov.au (or post it to The CEO, Southern Downs Regional Council, PO Box 26, Warwick QLD 4370).

Timing: objections must be lodged within 31 days of your rate notice's issue date (or longer if Council allows). The next half-yearly notices — the first showing NPPR categories — are expected to issue around 18 August 2026, which puts the objection window at roughly mid-August to mid-September for most ratepayers.

Your notice must nominate the category you believe the land belongs in, and set out the facts and circumstances supporting your claim.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council's NPPR information (updated August 2026), the 6 August 2026 media release, and the objection form (v5, 27 July 2026)

faqs.q: What evidence do I need to include with my objection?
faqs.a:
Evidence is mandatory — an objection without it is deemed incomplete and declined.

Proof you live at the property (required for a change to a residential/PPR category):

  • Confirmation of electoral enrolment at the address (check at check.aec.gov.au) plus one other legal document, or
  • Two or more current legal documents showing the address — e.g. electricity or telephone bill, vehicle registration renewal, insurance policy, or bank statement.

Proof the dwelling is lawful (where it applies):

  • Dwellings built after 1 January 2000 — Form 21 Final Inspection Certificate or equivalent
  • Dwellings built before 2000 — proof of the dwelling's age (building approval, aerial imagery, Form 21 or equivalent) and/or a Council building record search
  • Temporary homes — a copy of your current Permission to Occupy Temporary Accommodation
Properties currently recorded under vacant land use codes (01A/06A) must also include the Form 21 to show a lawful dwelling exists.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council's NPPR information (updated August 2026), the 6 August 2026 media release, and the objection form (v5, 27 July 2026)

faqs.q: What happens after I lodge my objection?
faqs.a:
Within 60 days of receiving your objection, the Chief Executive Officer reviews it and makes one of three decisions:

  • Assign the property to the land use and rating category you requested, or
  • Assign it to an alternative land use and/or rating category, or
  • Deny the objection.

You're notified of the outcome in writing. If you're not satisfied with the decision, you can appeal by filing a Notice of Appeal in the Land Court registry within 42 days of receiving the decision notice, in the form approved by the Land Court.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council's NPPR information (updated August 2026), the 6 August 2026 media release, and the objection form (v5, 27 July 2026)

faqs.q: Do I still have to pay my rates while the objection is being decided?
faqs.a:
Yes. Section 88(e) of the Local Government Regulation 2012 provides that you remain liable to pay the amount on your rate notice even while an objection is on foot — objecting does not pause payment.

Pay in full by the due date or you lose the 7.5% prompt-payment discount — the discount is not allowed on payments received after the due date, regardless of the objection outcome.

If your objection succeeds, your rates are adjusted and any overpayment is dealt with on your account.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council's NPPR information (updated August 2026), the 6 August 2026 media release, and the objection form (v5, 27 July 2026)

faqs.q: I can't afford the increase. What are my options?
faqs.a:
The main tool is a Payment Agreement, which offers rates relief by deferring all interest charges and legal recovery action from the date of application until 30 June of the current financial year. You can choose to pay weekly, fortnightly, monthly, or as a lump sum before 30 June.

Payment agreements are set up once your rates notice has issued — so when your notice arrives, call Council on 1300 697 372 to arrange one. See the Payment Agreements & Rates Relief page for details, including hardship provisions. There's also more general guidance under Rates & Payments.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council's NPPR information (updated August 2026), the 6 August 2026 media release, and the objection form (v5, 27 July 2026)

faqs.q: My land is used for primary production (farming). Is the objection form the right process?
faqs.a:
No. Moving into or out of a Primary Production rating category from any non-primary-production category isn't done with the objection form. Instead, an Application for Concessional Valuation (or notification that the land is no longer used for primary production) must be submitted to the Department of Natural Resources and Mines, Manufacturing and Regional and Rural Development — the application is available at www.resources.qld.gov.au.

If a new valuation is issued for your property, Council updates its records and your rating category accordingly.
faqs.lastReviewed: August 2026 — based on Council's NPPR information (updated August 2026), the 6 August 2026 media release, and the objection form (v5, 27 July 2026)

faqs.q: I disagree with the NPPR policy itself. How do I have my say?
faqs.a:
An objection only deals with whether your property's categorisation is factually correct — it isn't a vehicle for feedback on the policy. If you'd like to comment on the NPPR category as a policy decision, or on the objection process itself, lodge feedback through Council's formal feedback and complaints process (via an online service request or by contacting Council on 1300 697 372).

Council has said it welcomes community discussion on the change and will continue to answer questions raised at community meetings. In the meantime it's still worth checking your categorisation is correct — the three-part test above takes a minute, and Council staff can help you lodge an objection if your property has been miscategorised.

faqs.q: What dams can I visit in the Southern Downs?
faqs.a:
Council manages recreation areas at three dams, and each allows different activities.

  • Leslie Dam (Washpool Road, west of Warwick) — camping at Washpool Camping Reserve, plus swimming, boating, water skiing, sailing, canoeing and fishing.
  • Connolly Dam (Silverwood, south of Warwick) — camping, swimming and canoeing. Non-motorised craft only, though electric motors are allowed.
  • Storm King Dam (near Stanthorpe) — day use, boating and fishing. There is no camping at Storm King Dam.
Storm King Dam is occasionally closed to the public when the water is hired for a water sport competition. Spectators are still welcome on the foreshore.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to fish in the dams?
faqs.a:
Yes, if you are fishing a stocked impoundment. Leslie, Storm King and Connolly dams are stocked, and everyone aged 18 or over needs a Stocked Impoundment Permit Scheme (SIPS) permit before fishing them.

SIPS is a Queensland Government scheme, not a Council one. You can buy a permit online. The money goes toward maintaining and enhancing recreational fishing in stocked impoundments, and toward running the scheme.

Before you travel, check the Queensland Government's list of stocked impoundment locations. That list is the authority on which waters need a permit, and it is updated from time to time.

faqs.q: Can I take a boat out on the dams?
faqs.a:
Leslie Dam and Storm King Dam — yes. A separate Council boating permit is no longer required.

Connolly Dam — non-motorised craft such as canoes and kayaks only. Electric motors are permitted; petrol and other powered boats are not.

faqs.q: Where can I go fossicking?
faqs.a:
You need a fossicking licence from the Queensland Government before you fossick, and you can purchase one online.

A licence does not tell you where you may dig. Fossicking areas are designated by the State, and fossicking on private land also needs the landholder's permission. Confirm the area you are heading to is open before you travel.

faqs.q: Where can I camp in the region?
faqs.a:
Council runs two campgrounds, both at dams:

  • Washpool Camping Reserve at Leslie Dam — 80 sites, powered and unpowered. Bookings essential.
  • Connolly Dam Camping Ground — 20 unpowered sites, first come first served.

Short overnight stays are also allowed in three Council parks, covered further down this page.

For private and commercial campgrounds, see the Southern Downs & Granite Belt caravan, camping and holiday parks listing.

faqs.q: What's at Washpool Camping Reserve (Leslie Dam)?
faqs.a:
Washpool Camping Reserve sits at the southern end of Leslie Dam, at Washpool Road, Warwick 4370.

Sites: 34 powered and 46 unpowered, including drive-through sites for caravans of any size. Stays of up to seven nights. Check in after 12:00pm, check out before 11:00am.

Facilities: two toilet blocks with accessible facilities, hot and cold showers, a caravan dump point, clean drinking water and ice. Swimming, canoeing, water skiing, sailing and fishing (permit required).

Booking: essential. Call the Caretaker on 0427 026 216 between 12pm and 5pm, seven days a week. Online bookings are not available.

Full details are on the Washpool Reserve Camping Area page.

faqs.q: What's at Connolly Dam Camping Ground?
faqs.a:
Connolly Dam Camping Ground is at 1010 Connolly Dam Road, Silverwood, Warwick 4370. Part of Connolly Dam Road is gravel, and the access roads within the grounds are all gravel.

Sites: 20 unpowered grass sites suiting self-contained caravans and tent campers. Sites are not designated and are available first come, first served, for stays of up to seven days.

Facilities: one toilet block with accessible facilities, hot showers on a timer, a caravan dump point, swimming and non-motorised canoeing.

Booking: pre-booking is not available. The site runs on self-registration — look for the registration box with camping forms. Council officers visit daily to collect payment and check that campers have registered correctly.

Full details are on the Connolly Dam Camping Ground page.

faqs.q: What does camping cost?
faqs.a:
The same camping site fee applies at both Connolly Dam and Washpool Reserve, charged per camper per night.

WhoFee
Adult (18 and over), per night$15.80
Child (4 to 17 years), per night$8.50
Family (2 adults and up to 2 children under 18), per night$39.20
Children under 4Free
Powered site, in addition to the camping site fee$7.30

The overflow area at Washpool, for self-contained caravans and recreational vehicles, is charged at a lower rate.

Fees are set by Council each year and change on 1 July. The Fees & Charges schedule is always the current source.

faqs.q: Can I bring my dog?
faqs.a:
No. Dogs, cats and other domestic pets are not permitted at either Washpool Camping Reserve or Connolly Dam Camping Ground. Horses and livestock are not permitted either.

If you are travelling with a pet, the private caravan and holiday parks listed by Southern Downs & Granite Belt Tourism set their own rules — check directly with the park.

faqs.q: Can I have a campfire?
faqs.a:
Washpool Camping Reserve — yes, in the drums provided, and for cooking only. Firewood is not supplied, so bring your own. Bonfires and unattended fires are not permitted.

Connolly Dam Camping Ground — no. Campfires and bonfires are not permitted at any time.

Fire restrictions apply and can change at short notice. Check the current restrictions before lighting anything, including in a provided drum.

faqs.q: What are the campground rules?
faqs.a:
These apply at both Council campgrounds:

  • All flora and fauna is protected.
  • Vehicles must stay on formed roads and other designated areas.
  • A noise curfew applies from 10:30pm to 6:00am.
  • Camping is restricted to designated areas.

Not permitted at either campground: pets, horses and livestock; glass bottles; explosive devices and weapons; unregistered motor vehicles.

Washpool also: no bonfires or unattended fires, no camping or generators beyond the tree line, and no trespassing on neighbouring properties.

Connolly Dam also: no campfires at all, no camping beyond the high water mark, and no powered boats other than electric.

faqs.q: Can I camp at Storm King Dam?
faqs.a: No. There are no camping facilities at the Storm King Dam recreational facility and camping is not permitted there. There is a caravan park nearby.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight in a Council park?
faqs.a:
Yes, in three parks, for limited periods:

  • Dalrymple Creek Park, Allora Drive, Allora — 24 hours.
  • Leyburn Sports Grounds, Tummaville Road, Leyburn — 72 hours.
  • Jim Mitchell Park, McCosker Drive, Dalveen — 24 hours.

Tents and self-contained vehicles are both fine. Council displays signs in each park setting out how long you may stay, and the period on that notice is what applies.

These are rest stops rather than campgrounds — facilities are limited. For a longer stay, use one of the dam campgrounds or a private park.

faqs.q: Can I camp anywhere else — a roadside, reserve or car park?
faqs.a:
No. Under Council's Local Law No 4 (Local Government Controlled Areas, Facilities and Roads) 2011 and the matching Subordinate Local Law, camping, sleeping, occupying or remaining overnight in a local government controlled area is prohibited, unless the area is a park or reserve where camping is permitted by the notice displayed.

Local government controlled area: land, facilities and other infrastructure owned, held in trust or otherwise controlled by Council — anything other than a road.

faqs.q: Where are the caravan dump points?
faqs.a:
Council services five wastewater discharge points across the region:

  • Warwick — Morgan Park
  • Allora — Apex Park
  • Leyburn — Sports Ground
  • Dalveen — Jim Mitchell Park
  • Stanthorpe — Apex Park Reserve

Both Council campgrounds, Washpool Reserve and Connolly Dam, also have a dump point for campers staying there.

To use one, lift the lid of the discharge point and lower your wastewater hose into the receival point.

Only the three Ps go into a dump point — pee, poo and toilet paper. Wet wipes, rags, rubbish, children's toys, tennis balls, nappies, clothing, sanitary pads and tampons, cooking waste and sand all cause blockages and must not be discharged.

faqs.q: Where can I fill my water tanks?
faqs.a:
Council operates bulk water fill stations across the region. Locations, access and charges are on the Supply of Bulk Water page.

Washpool Camping Reserve also has clean drinking water available on site.

faqs.q: Where are the Visitor Information Centres?
faqs.a:
There are two, and both are worth a stop before you head out into the region.

Stanthorpe Visitor Information Centre
28 Leslie Parade, Stanthorpe
07 4681 2057
Monday to Sunday, 9am to 4pm
Ample parking directly in front of the Centre for all vehicle types.

Warwick Visitor Information Centre
Town Hall, 72 Palmerin Street, Warwick
07 4661 3122
Monday to Friday, 9am to 5pm; Saturday 9am to 4pm; Sunday 9am to 2pm
Parking on Palmerin Street or in the Council carpark off Fitzroy Street. Caravan and bus parking is available on Palmerin Street in front of Leslie Park.

More detail is on the Visitor Information Centres page.

faqs.q: What events are on?
faqs.a:
The Southern Downs & Granite Belt events listing carries what's on across the region, from food and wine events to markets and festivals.

For the region's agricultural shows and their dates, see Council's Agricultural Shows page.

faqs.q: Is Condamine River Road open?
faqs.a:
Road status changes with the weather, so check the Disaster Dashboard rather than relying on an earlier report. The Dashboard also carries flood cameras you can look at directly.

Never drive through floodwater, however shallow it looks. If a causeway is under water, turn around.

publishTabs.intro:
Visiting the Southern Downs? This tab covers the practical questions — where you can camp, what permits you need, where to empty a caravan tank — and points to the pages that go into detail.

Council runs the dam reserves, the two campgrounds and the dump points. Fishing and fossicking permits are Queensland Government schemes, and events, private caravan parks and general visitor information come from Southern Downs & Granite Belt Tourism.
